Neither clause, because the two clauses overlap and Python stops with a traceback instead.
Both clauses, because a missing file is both an OSError and a FileNotFoundError.
questions.why: Python checks clauses from top to bottom and the first match wins, so the general OSError clause takes the error and the specific clause is never reached.

questions.prompt: A payroll service wraps its pay-rate calculation in try: ... then except Exception: pass. A developer misspells a variable name inside the try block, so Python raises NameError on every run. In production, what is the most likely result?
choices: The NameError is swallowed, the service reports success while using wrong data, and the logs never show the typo.
The service crashes with a traceback that points at the misspelled line, because NameError is never caught.
Only Ctrl+C is affected, because except Exception catches KeyboardInterrupt but not NameError.
Python fixes the misspelled name automatically, because the except clause tells it to ignore errors.
questions.why: Exception is the parent of almost all ordinary errors, including NameError, so except Exception: pass hides the bug. The service keeps running on bad data, and the real cause never appears in the logs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why our config loader should catch FileNotFoundError rather than use a bare except. Name at least one situation where catching something broader, like OSError, would be reasonable, and say what that costs.
lessons.modelAnswer: Catching FileNotFoundError says exactly which failure we expect and have a plan for: if the file is missing, we load defaults. Anything else, like a typo that raises NameError, still stops the program with a traceback that points at the bug. A bare except would catch that typo too. We would silently run on defaults and never learn something was broken. It would even catch Ctrl+C and SystemExit, so the program could ignore someone trying to stop it. Catching OSError is reasonable if our recovery is the same for every file-access problem, such as a missing file or no permission. The cost is that we lose detail. If we do catch broadly, we should log which error happened so it is not hidden. We should also list specific clauses before general ones, because the first matching clause wins.
rubricPoints: States that a specific except catches only the named type and its subclasses, while a bare except catches everything.
Explains that broad catches hide unrelated bugs such as a NameError and leave the program running on wrong data.
Mentions that a bare except also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit.
Gives a fair case for a broader parent type such as OSError and names the loss of detail as its cost.
Notes that specific clauses must come before general ones because the first match wins.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner harden a config loader with error handling, which directly practises choosing which exception types to catch and which to let surface.

lessons.plain: A class is a blueprint that describes a kind of thing, and an instance is one actual thing built from that blueprint. Think of a cookie cutter and the cookies it makes: one cutter, many cookies, and each cookie can get its own icing. In programming, the details each thing holds (a server's name, whether it is up) are called attributes, and the actions it can perform (restart, report status) are called methods. Classes let you bundle data and the behaviour that works on that data together, so your program can describe real things like servers, users or orders in a tidy, reusable way.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you build two separate servers from the same blueprint and then mark only the first one as down, what do you expect the second server's status to be, and why?
lessons.teach:
A class is a named definition of a kind of object, written with the class keyword. An object is any value Python works with; an instance is an object created from a particular class, made by calling the class like a function, with parentheses: Server(). An attribute is a named value attached to an object, read and written with a dot, as in web.name. A method is a function defined inside a class that runs on one instance; you call it with a dot and parentheses, as in web.mark_down().

Why it works: each instance keeps its own set of attributes, so many instances can share one set of methods while holding different data. When you call a method, Python automatically passes the instance as the first argument, conventionally named self, so the method knows which object to change. (How self and setup work in detail is covered in its own lesson.)

Worked example. Suppose a class Server contains one method, mark_down, whose body sets self.up to False. Step 1: web = Server() creates an instance. Step 2: web.name = "web-1" and web.up = True attach two attributes to that instance. Step 3: db = Server(), then db.up = True, creates a second, independent instance. Step 4: web.mark_down() runs the method with self bound to web, so web.up becomes False. Step 5: checking db.up still gives True, because the method only changed the instance it was called on.

Common mistake: forgetting parentheses. Writing web = Server gives you the class itself, not a new instance, so attributes you set land on the blueprint and can appear shared everywhere. Similarly, writing web.mark_down without parentheses just refers to the method and never runs it, so nothing changes and no error is raised. In a running monitoring script, that silent bug means a failed server keeps reporting as healthy.

Classes package data and behaviour together, and each instance carries its own state.

questions.prompt: A help desk tool has a class Ticket containing one method, close, whose body sets self.status to "closed". Trace these steps. Step 1: t1 = Ticket() creates an instance. Step 2: t1.title = "Printer jam" and t1.status = "open" attach two attributes to it. Step 3: t2 = Ticket(), then t2.status = "open", creates a second, independent ticket. Step 4: (missing). Step 5: checking t1.status gives "closed", while t2.status still gives "open". Which line belongs in Step 4?
choices: t2.close()
Ticket.close
t1.close()
t1.close
questions.why: Calling close with parentheses on t1 runs the method with self bound to t1, so only t1's status changes and t2 keeps its own value.

questions.prompt: In Python, what is an attribute?
choices: A function defined inside a class that runs on one instance
The class keyword used to start a class definition
The first argument Python passes to every method
A named value attached to an object, read and written with a dot
questions.why: An attribute is a named value on an object, such as pump.flow, accessed with dot notation; a function defined in a class is a method instead.

questions.prompt: A water plant script has a class Pump with one method, start, whose body sets self.running to True. The script runs: p1 = Pump(), p2 = Pump(), p1.running = False, p2.running = False, then p2.start(). What are p1.running and p2.running afterwards?
choices: p1.running is False and p2.running is True
p1.running is True and p2.running is False
Both are True, because start belongs to the shared class
Both are False, because start was never really called
questions.why: Each instance keeps its own attributes, and p2.start() runs with self bound to p2, so only p2.running changes to True.

questions.prompt: A lab script is meant to create a new sensor object but contains the line sensor = Sensor (no parentheses), followed by sensor.unit = "C". What has actually happened?
choices: sensor refers to the class itself, so unit was set on the blueprint and can appear shared everywhere
Python raised an error because a class cannot be assigned to a variable
Nothing happened, because attributes can only be set inside methods
Python created a new, independent instance and stored unit on it as intended
questions.why: Without parentheses the class is not called, so sensor is just another name for the class and the attribute lands on the class rather than on a new instance.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a class and an instance, and between attributes and methods, using an example from your own work. Name one limit or pitfall, such as when a class is more structure than the problem needs, or the parentheses mistake.
lessons.modelAnswer: A class is the blueprint, like a definition of what a Server is; an instance is one concrete server built from it by calling Server() with parentheses. Attributes are the data an instance holds, such as its name or whether it is up, accessed with a dot. Methods are functions defined in the class that act on a specific instance; when I call web.mark_down(), Python passes web in as self, so only web changes and my db instance stays as it was. That separation of shared behaviour and per-instance data is the whole point. One pitfall: leaving off parentheses. Server without () is the class, not a new object, and web.mark_down without () never runs, silently. A tradeoff is that for a tiny script with one piece of data, a plain dictionary or function can be simpler than a class.
rubricPoints: A class is a blueprint; an instance is one object created by calling the class with parentheses.
Attributes are named values on an object, accessed with dot notation.
Methods are functions defined in the class that act on the instance they are called on.
Each instance keeps its own attribute values, so changing one does not change another.
Names a pitfall or limit, such as missing parentheses or a class being overkill for simple data.

suggested.rationale: No current mission has the learner define classes, so short hands-on drills creating instances, setting attributes and calling methods would build the skill best.

lessons.plain: When you build objects from a class, each object needs its own starting data. A special method called __init__ runs automatically the moment a new object is created, and its job is to fill in that object's details. Inside it, the word self means 'the particular object being set up right now'. Data stored on self belongs to one object only; data written directly in the class body is shared by every object. Think of a hotel. Each guest gets their own room key, like instance data. Everyone shares the same lobby, like class data.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a class defines a shopping list once, directly in the class body. Two separate objects are made from that class, and each one adds an item to that list. When you look at the second object's list, do you think it holds one item or two? Why?
lessons.teach:
An instance is one object made from a class. An attribute is a named value attached to something, read with a dot, as in truck.name. __init__ is the initializer: Python calls it automatically right after creating a new instance, passing that new instance as the first argument. By convention that first parameter is named self. Writing self.name = name inside __init__ attaches name to that one instance. This is an instance attribute, and every object gets its own copy.

A class attribute is assigned directly in the class body, outside any method. It lives on the class itself, so all instances share it. Lookup explains why: when you read obj.x, Python first checks the instance's own attributes. If x is not found there, it checks the class.

Worked example. Picture class Truck with wheels = 4 in the class body, and an __init__(self, name) that sets self.name = name and self.cargo = []. Now trace these steps. First, a = Truck('A') runs __init__ with self as the new object a. So a gets its own name 'A' and its own empty cargo list. Second, b = Truck('B') does the same for b, with a separate list. Third, a.cargo.append('boxes') changes only a's list, and b.cargo is still empty. Fourth, a.wheels and b.wheels both find nothing on the instance, fall back to the class, and return 4. Fifth, setting Truck.wheels = 6 changes the answer for both. Sixth, assigning a.wheels = 8 does not touch the class. It creates a new instance attribute on a that hides the class value, called shadowing, so b still sees 6.

Common mistake: putting a mutable value, one that can be changed in place such as a list or dict, in the class body, like cargo = []. Every instance then appends to the same single list. In a running program this shows up as data from one customer, request, or vehicle leaking into another, and it is a confusing bug to track down. Per-object state belongs in __init__ on self. Class attributes suit shared constants and settings.

questions.prompt: A weather service writes class Sensor. In the class body it puts unit = 'C'. Its __init__(self, sid) sets self.sid = sid and self.readings = []. Trace this. Step 1: s1 = Sensor(101) runs __init__ with self as the new object s1, so s1 gets its own sid 101 and its own empty readings list. Step 2: s2 = Sensor(102) does the same for s2, with a separate list. Step 3: s1.unit = 'F' runs. [MISSING: what this line does.] Step 4: Sensor.unit = 'K' runs. Now s2.unit returns 'K', but s1.unit still returns 'F'. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: It changes the class attribute on Sensor, so s2.unit and Sensor.unit both return 'F' from now on.
It creates an instance attribute unit on s1 that shadows the class value, so Sensor.unit and s2.unit stay 'C'.
It changes the class value only for Sensor objects created after this line, leaving s1 and s2 alone.
It raises an error, because unit was defined in the class body and cannot be set on one object.
questions.why: Assigning through an instance creates a new attribute on that one instance, which hides the class value, so the class and s2 are untouched. This is why Step 4 changes s2 but not s1.

questions.prompt: Inside a class Ticket, the method is written as def __init__(self, seat): self.seat = seat. When a program runs t = Ticket('12B'), what is self during that call?
choices: The new Ticket object that was just created, which Python passes in automatically as the first argument.
The string '12B', because it is the first value written inside the parentheses.
The Ticket class itself, so self.seat sets one value that every ticket shares.
A Python keyword that must appear exactly as self, or the method will not run at all.
questions.why: Python creates the new instance and then calls __init__ automatically, passing that instance as the first argument. By convention that parameter is named self.

questions.prompt: A shop writes class Order with items = [] in the class body. It also has a method add(self, thing) that runs self.items.append(thing). The program runs o1 = Order(), o2 = Order(), and then o1.add('lamp'). Printing o2.items shows ['lamp']. What explains this, and what is the fix?
choices: The append method copies values to every instance. The fix is to use a dict instead of a list.
o2 was created after o1, so it inherited o1's data. The fix is to create both orders at the same time.
Lists cannot be attributes. The fix is to store items as a single comma-separated string on the class.
items is a class attribute, so both orders share one list. The fix is to set self.items = [] inside __init__.
questions.why: A mutable value in the class body is one shared object. self.items finds it on the class and appends to it, so per-object state must be created on self in __init__.

questions.prompt: A bank writes class Account with rate = 0.02 in the class body. Its __init__(self, owner) sets self.owner = owner. The program runs acc1 = Account('Ravi'), acc2 = Account('Mei'), then Account.rate = 0.03, then acc2.rate = 0.05. What do acc1.rate, acc2.rate and Account.rate return now, in that order?
questions.why: acc1 has no rate of its own, so it falls back to the class value 0.03. The assignment acc2.rate = 0.05 creates a shadowing instance attribute on acc2 only and leaves the class value at 0.03.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why their two objects seem to share data they never meant to share. In your own words, explain what __init__ and self do. Explain the difference between instance and class attributes, and how Python looks up an attribute. Name one tradeoff or limit of using class attributes.
lessons.modelAnswer: __init__ is the method Python runs automatically right after it creates a new object. It receives that new object as self, so self.x = value stores x on that one object only. That is an instance attribute, and each object has its own. A value assigned directly in the class body is a class attribute: there is one copy, stored on the class and shared by every instance. When you read obj.x, Python looks on the instance first, then falls back to the class. Your bug is probably a list defined in the class body. Every object appends to that same list. Move it into __init__ as self.items = []. The tradeoff: class attributes are handy for shared constants and save repeating values, but they are dangerous when mutable. Also, assigning obj.x = something creates an instance attribute that shadows the class one rather than changing it for everyone.
rubricPoints: __init__ runs automatically when a new instance is created, to set up its starting state.
self refers to the specific instance being created or used.
Instance attributes are set on self and belong to one object; class attributes are set in the class body and are shared.
Attribute lookup checks the instance first, then the class.
Mutable class attributes such as lists are shared across all instances, a common source of bugs.
Assigning to an attribute on an instance creates a shadowing instance attribute rather than changing the class value.

suggested.rationale: The shared-mutable-class-attribute surprise and the shadowing rule stick best when the learner runs small drills, predicts the output, and sees the actual output for themselves.

lessons.plain: Inheritance lets you build a new class on top of an existing one. The new class, called the child, automatically gets every attribute and method of the original, called the parent. The child can then add new abilities or replace some of the parent's behaviour with its own version, which is called overriding. When the child's replacement still needs the parent's original work done, it calls super() to borrow it. Think of a family recipe: you copy grandma's soup, keep most steps, swap one ingredient, and still follow her original method for the broth instead of rewriting it from scratch.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a parent class has a method called send(), and a child class also defines its own method called send(). If you create an object from the child class and call send() on it, which version do you think runs, and why might that be useful?
lessons.teach:
Inheritance means one class (the child or subclass) is defined in terms of another (the parent or base class), written class Child(Parent). The child receives all of the parent's methods and attributes without retyping them. Method overriding means the child defines a method with the same name as one in the parent; the child's version wins. super() is a built-in that returns a stand-in for the parent, so super().method() runs the parent's version from inside the child.

Why it works: when you call obj.send(), Python looks for send on the object's own class first, then on its parent, then further up. This search order is called the method resolution order. The first match is used, so a child definition hides the parent's.

Worked example. Alert has __init__(self, message) that stores self.message, and send(self) that returns "ALERT: " + self.message. PagerAlert(Alert) defines __init__(self, message, oncall) that calls super().__init__(message), then stores self.oncall. Its send(self) returns super().send() + " -> paging " + self.oncall.
Trace PagerAlert("disk full", "Ana").send(): step 1, PagerAlert.__init__ runs; super().__init__ sets self.message to "disk full"; then self.oncall becomes "Ana". Step 2, send is found on PagerAlert first, so its version runs. Step 3, super().send() runs Alert's send, giving "ALERT: disk full". Step 4, the child appends text, giving "ALERT: disk full -> paging Ana".

Common mistake: overriding __init__ in the child and forgetting to call super().__init__. The parent's setup never runs, so self.message is never created. Nothing fails at creation time; the program crashes later with an AttributeError the first time send() reads self.message, often far from the real cause in a running service.

questions.prompt:
A library app has a base class Report. Its __init__(self, title) stores self.title, and its render(self) returns "Report: " + self.title. A subclass SalesReport(Report) defines __init__(self, title, region), which calls super().__init__(title) and then stores self.region. Its render(self) returns super().render() + " [" + self.region + "]".

Trace SalesReport("Q3", "North").render().
Step 1: SalesReport.__init__ runs. super().__init__("Q3") sets self.title to "Q3", then self.region becomes "North".
Step 2: Python looks for render on SalesReport first, finds it there, and runs the child's version.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The child adds " [North]", so the final result is "Report: Q3 [North]".

What happens in Step 3?
choices: super().render() returns just "Q3", because the parent only stores the title
super().render() runs SalesReport's render again and returns "Report: Q3 [North]"
super().render() raises an AttributeError because self.title was never set
super().render() runs Report's render and returns "Report: Q3"
questions.why: super() stands in for the parent, so super().render() runs Report's version, which returns "Report: " + self.title, giving "Report: Q3".

questions.prompt: A fleet system has class Vehicle with describe(self) returning "generic vehicle". class Truck(Vehicle) defines its own describe(self) returning "heavy truck" and does not call super(). class Van(Vehicle) defines no methods at all. What do Truck().describe() and Van().describe() return?
choices: "generic vehicle" and "generic vehicle"
"generic vehicle" and "heavy truck"
"heavy truck" and an AttributeError
"heavy truck" and "generic vehicle"
questions.why: Python checks the object's own class first: Truck has its own describe, which overrides the parent's, while Van has none, so the search moves up to Vehicle and uses its inherited version.

questions.prompt: In a billing service, class Invoice has __init__(self, amount) that stores self.amount, and total(self) that returns self.amount * 1.2. A developer writes class RushInvoice(Invoice) with __init__(self, amount, fee) that stores only self.fee and never calls super().__init__. What happens when the service runs inv = RushInvoice(100, 15) and later calls inv.total()?
choices: inv.total() returns 120, because amount is inherited automatically
inv.total() returns 135, because the fee is added in
The object is created without error, but inv.total() crashes with an AttributeError because self.amount was never set
Creating the object fails immediately with a TypeError
questions.why: Overriding __init__ without calling super().__init__ skips the parent's setup, so self.amount is never created; nothing fails at creation, and the error appears only when total() first reads self.amount.

questions.prompt: At a bank, class Account has withdraw(self, amount), which checks the balance and subtracts the money. You write class SavingsAccount(Account) and override withdraw so it first checks a monthly limit and then performs the normal withdrawal exactly as Account does. Inside SavingsAccount.withdraw, which line should perform that normal withdrawal?
choices: withdraw(amount)
self.withdraw(amount)
super().withdraw(amount)
SavingsAccount.withdraw(self, amount)
questions.why: super().withdraw(amount) runs the parent's version, while self.withdraw or SavingsAccount.withdraw would find the child's own method first and call it again instead of the parent's.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what happens when a child class overrides a method and calls super() inside it. Include one risk or limit of relying on inheritance this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: When a class inherits from another, it gets all the parent's methods for free. If the child defines a method with the same name, Python finds the child's version first, because it searches the object's own class before moving up to the parent; that is overriding. Inside the override, super() hands you the parent's version, so you can reuse its work and only add what is different, like a pager alert that builds the normal alert text and then appends who is being paged. The big risk is forgetting super().__init__ when you override the constructor: the parent's attributes are never set, and the code breaks later with an AttributeError somewhere confusing. A broader limit is that the child is tightly tied to the parent, so changing the parent can silently change every child.
rubricPoints: Child classes automatically receive the parent's methods and attributes.
Overriding means the child defines a same-named method, and Python finds the child's version first.
super() calls the parent's version so the child can extend rather than rewrite it.
Forgetting super().__init__ leaves parent attributes unset and causes later errors.
Names a limit such as tight coupling between child and parent.

suggested.rationale: No current mission exercises class hierarchies, and a Python drill where the learner overrides methods and fixes a missing super().__init__ would build the skill by doing.

lessons.plain: Composition and inheritance are two ways to reuse code between classes. Inheritance means a new class is a special kind of an existing class, so it automatically gets the parent's behaviour. Composition means a class holds another object inside it and asks that object to do part of the work. Think of a delivery van. A van is a kind of vehicle, which is inheritance. A van has an engine, which is composition. Most of the skill is noticing which relationship you really have. When in doubt, prefer has-a, because parts are easier to swap than family trees are to change.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a Server class that needs to send alert emails. Would you make Server a child of an EmailSender class, or give each Server an EmailSender object to use? Which would make it easier to switch alerts to a chat app later?
lessons.teach:
Inheritance is when a class, called the child or subclass, is built on another class, called the parent or base class. The child automatically gets the parent's attributes, which are data stored on the object, and its methods, which are functions attached to the object. It fits an is-a relationship: a DatabaseServer is a Server.

Composition is when a class keeps another object as one of its attributes and delegates to it. To delegate means to hand a job to that inner object by calling its method. It fits a has-a relationship: a Server has a notifier.

Why prefer composition by default? Inheritance couples the child tightly to the parent. A change in the parent ripples into every child, and a class can only sensibly be one kind of thing. Composition keeps pieces separate, so you can replace a part without touching the class that uses it.

Here is a worked example. Server.__init__ stores self.notifier = EmailNotifier(). Server.check() finds the disk full and calls self.notifier.send('disk full'). EmailNotifier.send then emails the on-call engineer. Later the team moves to a chat tool. You write a ChatNotifier class with its own send method and create the server with ChatNotifier() instead. Server itself does not change. The only requirement is that every notifier offers a send method.

A common mistake is inheriting just to borrow a method, for example class Server(EmailNotifier). A Server is not an email notifier. It ends up exposing email methods it should not have. Switching to chat would mean rewriting the class hierarchy, and testing a Server would send real emails unless you work around the parent.

In a running system, misused inheritance makes small changes risky, because editing a base class can quietly break many subclasses. Good composition lets you swap a part, such as a fake notifier in tests, safely. Use inheritance when the child truly is a specialised version of the parent and should be usable anywhere the parent is expected. Otherwise, compose.

questions.prompt: A bakery's online shop has an OrderSystem class. Step 1: OrderSystem.__init__ stores self.payment = CardProcessor(). Step 2: OrderSystem.checkout(42) calls self.payment.charge(42), and CardProcessor.charge takes 42 pounds from the customer's card. Step 3: The bakery now also wants to accept gift vouchers. Step 4: ??? Step 5: OrderSystem.checkout still just calls self.payment.charge(total), and the OrderSystem class itself is not edited. Which choice correctly fills Step 4?
choices: Make OrderSystem inherit from CardProcessor and override charge so it can handle vouchers as well as cards
Write a VoucherProcessor class with its own charge method, and create the OrderSystem with VoucherProcessor() in place of CardProcessor()
Add an if/else inside OrderSystem.checkout that charges a card or a voucher depending on a flag
Make VoucherProcessor inherit from OrderSystem so it gets the checkout method and can charge vouchers
questions.why: With composition, OrderSystem only relies on its payment part having a charge method, so you swap in a new part with the same method and OrderSystem needs no change, which is exactly what Step 5 says happens.

questions.prompt: Which of these relationships is the best fit for inheritance rather than composition?
choices: A Robot class that needs power from a Battery
A SavingsAccount class that is a specialised BankAccount and should work anywhere a BankAccount is expected
A Game class that needs to write messages using a Logger
An Invoice class that needs to turn itself into a PDF using a PdfExporter
questions.why: Inheritance fits a true is-a relationship where the child can be used anywhere the parent is expected; the other three are has-a relationships, where the class uses a part, so they call for composition.

questions.prompt: A developer writes class Spreadsheet(CsvWriter) only so that Spreadsheet can reuse CsvWriter's save method. What is the main problem with this design?
choices: Spreadsheet now exposes CSV-writer methods it should not have, and moving to a different file format would mean reworking the class hierarchy
Every Spreadsheet object will run more slowly, because inherited methods take longer to call
There is no problem, because inheriting to borrow a method is the usual way to share code
Python will raise an error, because a class may not inherit from a class that writes files
questions.why: A Spreadsheet is not a CSV writer, so inheriting just to borrow one method couples it tightly to that parent, leaks unrelated methods into it and makes swapping the saving approach hard.

questions.prompt: A WeatherStation class stores self.alerter = SmsAlerter() and calls self.alerter.send_alert(message) when a storm is detected. The team wants automated tests that never send real text messages. Which approach follows the composition idea?
choices: Delete the alert call from WeatherStation while the tests run, then add it back before release
Edit SmsAlerter so that it checks whether a test is running before it sends anything
Make WeatherStation inherit from SmsAlerter and then override send_alert inside every test file
Give the WeatherStation a fake alerter object that has a send_alert method but records the message instead of texting
questions.why: Because WeatherStation only depends on its alerter part having a send_alert method, a fake part can be swapped in for tests without changing WeatherStation or the real SmsAlerter.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide between inheritance and composition for a new class, using an example from your own work. Name one limit or cost of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking whether the relationship is is-a or has-a. If a DatabaseServer really is a Server and could be used anywhere a Server is expected, inheritance is fine. It gives me the parent's methods for free and lets me override only what differs. The cost is tight coupling, because a change to the parent affects every child and the hierarchy is hard to reshape later. If the relationship is has-a, like a Server that has a notifier, I use composition. I store the notifier as an attribute and call its send method. That lets me swap email for chat, or drop in a fake for tests, without touching Server. The cost of composition is a bit more wiring, such as passing in the part and writing small delegating calls. I also have to keep the parts' method names consistent. My default is composition unless the is-a test clearly passes.
rubricPoints: Defines inheritance as an is-a relationship where the child gets the parent's attributes and methods.
Defines composition as a has-a relationship where an object holds another object and delegates work to it.
Gives a concrete example showing which relationship fits and why.
Names the coupling cost of inheritance: parent changes ripple into children and the hierarchy is hard to change.
Names a cost of composition, such as extra wiring or the need for a consistent interface between swappable parts.
States a sensible default: prefer composition unless the is-a relationship genuinely holds.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is judging and justifying which relationship fits a problem, and no current mission exercises Python class design, so explaining the choice back is the most direct practice.

lessons.plain: Python has a set of special method names wrapped in double underscores on each side, nicknamed dunder methods (short for double underscore). You never call them directly. Python calls them for you when you use a built-in operation on your object, such as printing it, comparing two objects with double equals, or asking how long something is. Think of them as sockets on a wall: the plug (print, comparison, length) is standard, and by writing a dunder method you decide what your object does when something is plugged in. Four common ones control how an object describes itself to users, how it describes itself to developers, when two objects count as equal, and what its length is.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you make two separate objects from your own class with exactly the same data and compare them with ==, do you think Python will say True or False by default, and why?
lessons.teach:
A dunder method is a method whose name starts and ends with two underscores. Python's built-in functions and operators look for these names on your class and call them.

__str__ returns a friendly, readable string for end users. print(obj) and str(obj) call it. __repr__ returns an unambiguous string for developers, ideally one that looks like code that would rebuild the object. The interactive prompt, debuggers, and containers such as lists call it. If you define only __repr__, Python also uses it for str(), so __repr__ is the one to write first.

__eq__(self, other) decides what == means. Without it, == checks identity, meaning whether both names point to the very same object in memory, so two separate objects with equal data compare False. __len__(self) must return a non-negative whole number. len(obj) calls it, and an object whose length is 0 counts as false in an if statement.

Worked example: a Playlist class stores a name and a list of song titles. Its __repr__ returns "Playlist('Gym', ['A', 'B'])". Its __str__ returns "Gym (2 songs)". Its __eq__ first checks that other is a Playlist; if not, it returns NotImplemented, a special value telling Python to try the other object's comparison or fall back to identity. Otherwise it compares names and song lists. Its __len__ returns the number of songs. Trace it: p = Playlist('Gym', ['A','B']); q = Playlist('Gym', ['A','B']). print(p) shows Gym (2 songs). [p] shows [Playlist('Gym', ['A', 'B'])] because lists use repr. p == q calls p.__eq__(q), the names and songs match, so the result is True. len(p) returns 2.

Common mistake: defining __eq__ and then trying to put the objects in a set or use them as dictionary keys. Python sets __hash__ to None once you define __eq__, so the object becomes unhashable and raises TypeError, unless you also define __hash__ consistently with equality. In a running system, this surfaces as a crash the first time code deduplicates those objects.

questions.prompt: A school's timetabling tool has a Roster class that stores a course name and a list of student names. Its __repr__ returns "Roster('Chem', ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Cy'])" and its __str__ returns "Chem: 3 students". Trace it: r = Roster('Chem', ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Cy']). Step 1: print(r) shows Chem: 3 students, because print calls __str__. Step 2: shelf = [r], then print(shelf) shows ______. Step 3: len(r) returns 3, because __len__ returns the number of students. What belongs in the blank in Step 2?
choices: Chem: 3 students, because a one-item list is shown as its single item
[Roster('Chem', ['Ana', 'Bo', 'Cy'])], because a list shows its items using __repr__
[<Roster object>], because lists ignore dunder methods defined on your class
[Chem: 3 students], because print always uses __str__ for everything it displays
questions.why: Printing a list displays each item inside it with that item's __repr__, not its __str__, so the code-like string appears inside square brackets.

questions.prompt: A warehouse app has a Pallet class. The developer wrote only a __repr__ method, which returns "Pallet('P-17', 40)". There is no __str__ method. What does str(Pallet('P-17', 40)) return?
choices: An empty string, because no friendly text was defined
"Pallet('P-17', 40)", because Python falls back to __repr__ when __str__ is missing
An error, because str() requires a __str__ method to exist
The same text as the == comparison of two pallets
questions.why: When only __repr__ is defined, Python uses it for str() as well, which is why __repr__ is the one to write first.

questions.prompt: A print shop has a JobQueue class whose __len__ returns how many print jobs are waiting. Right now no jobs are waiting, so __len__ returns 0. What does this code print? if queue: print('busy') else: print('idle')
choices: idle, because an object whose length is 0 counts as false
busy, because the queue object exists
Nothing, because if cannot test a custom object
A TypeError, because __len__ returned 0
questions.why: An object whose __len__ returns 0 is treated as false in an if statement, so the else branch runs.

questions.prompt: A mapping service defines a GridPoint class with an __eq__ method that compares x and y values, but no __hash__ method. Later, code runs unique = {GridPoint(4, 9), GridPoint(4, 9)} to remove duplicate points. What happens?
choices: A TypeError is raised, because defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None and makes the objects unhashable
The set is built, but every later == check between the points returns False
The set holds two points, because == falls back to checking identity
The set holds one point, because __eq__ says the two points are equal
questions.why: Once __eq__ is defined without a matching __hash__, Python sets __hash__ to None, so putting the objects in a set raises TypeError.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what __str__, __repr__, __eq__ and __len__ each do and which built-in triggers each one, and name one tradeoff or pitfall that comes with defining __eq__.
lessons.modelAnswer: These are hooks Python calls for us. __str__ is the readable version used by print and str(), meant for users. __repr__ is the precise developer version used by the interactive prompt, debuggers and when the object sits inside a list; if only __repr__ exists, str() falls back to it, so I write that one first. __eq__ defines ==; without it, == only checks whether two names refer to the same object, so equal-looking copies compare False. Inside __eq__ I return NotImplemented when the other object is a different type. __len__ backs len() and must return a non-negative integer; a zero length also makes the object falsy in an if. The pitfall: once I define __eq__, Python removes the default hash, so the objects can no longer go into sets or be dict keys unless I add a matching __hash__.
rubricPoints: Dunder methods are called by Python through built-ins and operators, not called directly.
__str__ is the user-friendly form for print/str; __repr__ is the unambiguous developer form and is the fallback for str.
Without __eq__, == compares identity; __eq__ lets equal data compare True and should return NotImplemented for unrelated types.
__len__ backs len(), must return a non-negative integer, and zero length makes the object falsy.
Defining __eq__ removes the default hash, breaking set and dict-key use unless __hash__ is also defined.

suggested.rationale: Writing a small class and watching print, ==, len and a set call its dunder methods makes the triggers and the hash pitfall concrete in a way reading cannot.

lessons.plain: Encapsulation means an object keeps its inner workings to itself and offers a small, deliberate set of ways to use it. Python has no hard lock for this. Instead it relies on naming habits. A name starting with one underscore says 'internal, please leave it alone.' A name starting with two underscores gets quietly renamed so that a child class cannot clash with it by accident. A property lets something look like a plain value while a check runs behind the scenes. Think of a bank teller window: you ask for your balance or make a deposit, but you never reach into the vault yourself.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a Python class stores a value in an attribute named with two leading underscores, do you think code outside the class can still read it somehow, or is it truly locked away? Make a guess.
lessons.teach:
Encapsulation means hiding an object's internal data behind a small, deliberate interface, so outside code neither depends on those details nor breaks them. Python has no enforced private keyword. It uses naming conventions plus one small language feature.

A single leading underscore, as in self._balance, is a convention meaning 'internal, do not use from outside.' Python does nothing to stop access. It is a signal to other programmers, and linters (tools that check code style) warn about it.

A double leading underscore with no trailing underscores, as in self.__token, triggers name mangling. Inside class Account, Python rewrites that name to _Account__token. The purpose is to prevent accidental clashes when a subclass uses the same attribute name. It does not hide secrets, because anyone can still type obj._Account__token.

A property is a method that you read like a plain attribute. Putting @property above a method named balance makes reading obj.balance call that method, which is called the getter. Adding a method marked @balance.setter makes obj.balance = 50 call your setter, where you can validate the new value. This lets you start with a plain attribute and add checks later without changing any calling code.

Worked example: Account keeps the real value in self._balance. The balance getter returns self._balance. The setter raises ValueError if the new value is negative and otherwise stores it in self._balance. Trace acct.balance = -5. Python sees that balance is a property and calls the setter with -5. The check fails, so ValueError is raised and _balance keeps its old value. Next, acct.balance = 20 runs the setter, the check passes, and _balance becomes 20. Reading acct.balance then calls the getter, which returns 20.

Common mistake: writing self.balance = value inside the setter instead of self._balance = value. That line calls the setter again, over and over, until Python raises RecursionError, and in a running service that request crashes. A second mistake is treating double underscores as security. They keep nothing secret, so never rely on them to protect passwords or keys.

questions.prompt: A greenhouse company writes a class Thermostat. It keeps the real target temperature in self._target. The target getter, marked @property, returns self._target. The setter, marked @target.setter, raises ValueError if the new value is below 10 or above 30. Otherwise it does one more thing, shown as the missing line. Trace t.target = 22. Python sees that target is a property and calls the setter with 22. The check passes, and the missing line runs. Reading t.target then calls the getter, which returns 22. Which line belongs in the gap?
choices: self._target = value
self.__target = value
self.target = value
return value
questions.why: Storing into self._target keeps the value where the getter reads it without going back through the property, so later reads of t.target return 22.

questions.prompt: Inside a class named Sensor, a method runs self.__key = 'abc'. The name has two leading underscores and no trailing underscores. Under what name does Python actually store this attribute on the object?
choices: _key, with one underscore removed
__key, exactly as written
_Sensor__key
key, with all underscores removed
questions.why: A double leading underscore with no trailing underscores triggers name mangling, which rewrites the name to an underscore, the class name, and the original name.

questions.prompt: A logistics team's Route class stores data in self._cache. A script outside the class reads route._cache directly. What happens when the script runs?
choices: Python raises AttributeError because the attribute is private
Python silently returns None in place of the real value
The read works; the underscore is only a convention, though a linter may warn
The read works only if the script is in a subclass of Route
questions.why: A single leading underscore signals 'internal, do not use from outside', but Python does nothing to block access. Linters, which are tools that check code style, may flag it.

questions.prompt: A developer at a payments startup stores an API key in self.__api_key and says the key is now hidden from any code outside the class. What is the accurate response?
choices: True: double underscores make the attribute fully private in Python
True, but only once a @property getter is also added for it
Not true: the key is deleted when the object leaves its own class
Not true: the name is only mangled, so anyone can still read obj._ClassName__api_key
questions.why: Name mangling exists to prevent accidental name clashes with subclasses, not to keep secrets, because the mangled name is still reachable from outside.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a single underscore, a double underscore, and a property in a Python class, and name one limit of these tools, such as what they cannot protect against.
lessons.modelAnswer: Python has no real private attributes, so we use signals. One leading underscore, like _balance, is purely a convention meaning 'internal, don't touch.' Nothing stops you, but linters and reviewers will flag it. Two leading underscores, like __token, make Python rename the attribute to _ClassName__token. That exists mainly so a subclass doesn't accidentally overwrite the parent's attribute. A property lets callers write obj.balance as if it were a plain attribute, while a getter or setter method actually runs. That is how you add validation later without changing calling code. Usually the property stores the real value in an underscored attribute. The limit is that none of this is security. Anyone can still reach _balance or _Account__token, so it guards against accidents, not against attackers. Also, the setter must assign to self._balance and not self.balance, or it calls itself forever.
rubricPoints: States that a single underscore is only a convention that Python does not enforce.
Explains that a double underscore triggers name mangling to _ClassName__name, mainly to avoid clashes in subclasses.
Describes a property as a method that is accessed like an attribute, with an optional setter for validation.
Notes that properties let you add checks later without changing calling code.
Names a limit: these conventions are not security, and the data is still reachable.
Mentions the setter recursion pitfall or the need for a separate underscored storage attribute.

suggested.rationale: Writing a property with a validating setter and watching name mangling happen is best learned by running small Python exercises, which no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: A module is simply a Python file whose code you can reuse in another file, and a package is a folder that groups related modules together. Importing means telling Python, at the top of your file, "bring in that code so I can use it here." Think of a library building: an absolute import gives the full address from the front door (building, floor, shelf), while a relative import says "the shelf next to this one." Full addresses work from anywhere. Short directions only make sense if you know where you are standing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your project has a folder called shop containing two files, cart.py and prices.py. Inside cart.py you want to use a function from prices.py. Can you guess two different ways you might describe where prices.py is, one starting from the top of the project and one starting from cart.py's own location?
lessons.teach:
An import statement loads code from another file so you can use its names. A module is one .py file. A package is a folder of modules that Python treats as a unit, usually marked by an __init__.py file. When you write import x, Python searches a list of folders called sys.path, which normally starts with the folder of the script you launched, then the standard library and installed libraries. The first match wins.

An absolute import names the full dotted path from a top-level package, such as from shop.prices import tax. A relative import names a location relative to the current module's package using leading dots. One dot means "my own package" and two dots mean "the parent package," so from .prices import tax and from ..utils import log are relative imports. Relative imports work only inside a package, because Python needs to know which package the current file belongs to.

Worked example: a project folder holds main.py and a package folder shop, which contains __init__.py, cart.py and prices.py. You run python main.py from the project folder. That folder is added to sys.path. main.py runs from shop.cart import total. Python finds the shop folder, loads cart.py, and cart.py runs from .prices import tax. The dot resolves to shop, so Python loads shop.prices, finds tax, and everything works.

Common mistake: running python shop/cart.py directly. Python then treats cart.py as a standalone script with no parent package, so the relative import fails with "attempted relative import with no known parent package." The fix is to run it as a module from the project folder with python -m shop.cart. A related trap is naming your own file after a standard library module, such as random.py. Your file is found first and hides the real one. In a running system, imports that depend on which folder you launched from will pass on your laptop and then crash in a deployment that starts the program differently. Absolute imports from a clear top-level package are the safer default.

questions.prompt: A team builds a project folder that holds run.py and a package folder called clinic. Inside clinic are __init__.py, billing.py (which defines a function invoice) and a subpackage folder visits, which has its own __init__.py plus booking.py. They launch with python run.py from the project folder, so that folder goes on sys.path. run.py runs from clinic.visits.booking import book, and Python loads booking.py as clinic.visits.booking. Missing step: booking.py needs invoice from billing.py, using a relative import. Which line should booking.py contain?
choices: from .billing import invoice
import clinic.visits.billing
from ..billing import invoice
from billing import invoice
questions.why: booking.py's own package is clinic.visits, so two dots point to the parent package clinic, where billing.py lives.

questions.prompt: In Python, what is the difference between a module and a package?
choices: A module is a folder of .py files; a package is one .py file that has been installed from the internet.
A module is one .py file; a package is a folder of modules treated as a unit, usually marked by an __init__.py file.
A module can only use absolute imports; a package can only use relative imports between its files.
A module is any file in the standard library; a package is any file you write yourself for a project.
questions.why: A module is a single .py file, while a package is a folder of modules that Python handles together, normally marked with __init__.py.

questions.prompt: A data analyst saves a helper script as statistics.py in the same folder as report.py, then runs python report.py. Inside report.py, the line import statistics is meant to load the standard library module, but calls to its functions fail. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The standard library statistics module must be installed separately before it can be imported.
import statistics only works inside a package folder that contains an __init__.py file.
report.py needs a relative import such as from .statistics import mean to reach the standard library.
The script's own folder comes first on sys.path, so the analyst's statistics.py is found first and hides the real module.
questions.why: Python searches sys.path in order starting with the launched script's folder, and the first match wins, so the local file shadows the standard library one.

questions.prompt: A project folder contains a package garden with __init__.py, planner.py and soil.py. planner.py contains from .soil import moisture. A developer runs python garden/planner.py and gets "attempted relative import with no known parent package." What fixes it?
choices: From the project folder, run python -m garden.planner so planner.py is loaded as part of the garden package.
Change the line to from ..soil import moisture so Python looks one level higher.
Move planner.py out of the garden folder so it sits next to the project folder.
Rename soil.py to __init__.py so planner.py can find it without a package.
questions.why: Running the file directly makes it a standalone script with no parent package, while python -m garden.planner loads it as a module inside garden so the dot resolves.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an absolute and a relative import, how Python decides where to find an imported module, and one situation where a relative import breaks.
lessons.modelAnswer: Importing loads names from another module, which is a single .py file, or from a package, which is a folder of modules. Python looks for the module in sys.path, a list of folders that starts with the launched script's folder and then covers the standard library and installed packages. The first match wins. That is why a file called random.py in your project can hide the real random module. An absolute import spells out the full path from the top-level package, like from shop.prices import tax, so it reads clearly and works the same from anywhere in the project. A relative import uses dots, like from .prices import tax, which is shorter and survives renaming the outer package. The tradeoff is that it only works when the file is loaded as part of a package. If you run cart.py directly as a script, there is no parent package and the import fails. Running python -m shop.cart fixes it.
rubricPoints: Defines a module as a file and a package as a folder of modules.
Explains that Python searches sys.path in order and uses the first match.
Describes an absolute import as the full dotted path from a top-level package.
Describes a relative import as dot notation based on the current package.
Names the limit that relative imports fail when a file is run directly as a script.
Mentions a fix or safer default, such as python -m or preferring absolute imports.

suggested.rationale: Import errors are best understood by arranging a small package, running it in different ways, and watching which imports resolve, which a Python drills engine could provide.

lessons.plain: A module is simply one Python file holding related code, like one chapter of a book. A package is a folder that groups several modules under one name, like a binder holding related chapters. In a traditional package, a special file named __init__.py sits inside the folder and tells Python to treat the folder as one named unit; it also runs once when the package is first loaded. Splitting a growing project this way keeps each file small and focused. It also lets two files share a name without clashing, because each lives in its own folder.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine your single 2,000-line script has grown to hold file reading, number crunching and report printing all mixed together. If you split it into several files and grouped them in one named folder, what everyday problems do you think that would solve?
lessons.teach:
A module is a single .py file; its name is the filename without the extension, so parsing.py is the module parsing. A package is a directory that holds modules (and possibly smaller packages, called subpackages) and contains a file named __init__.py. That file marks the folder as a regular package. It can be empty, and when it is not, its code runs once, the first time the package is imported, which means loaded into a running program.

Why it works: Python gives each module and package its own namespace, a separate set of names. A function called load inside fleetreport/parsing.py never collides with a load somewhere else, because its full name is fleetreport.parsing.load. Grouping by purpose also means a reader finds code by its folder and file name.

Worked example. Suppose you have main.py next to a folder fleetreport containing __init__.py, parsing.py and report.py. main.py runs import fleetreport.parsing. Step 1: Python finds the folder fleetreport and sees __init__.py, so it treats the folder as a package. Step 2: it runs __init__.py and creates the package object. Step 3: it finds parsing.py inside, runs that file's top-level code, and attaches it as fleetreport.parsing. Step 4: if report.py later imports the same package, Python reuses the copy it already loaded and does not run __init__.py again.

A common use of __init__.py is to re-export the most useful names, for example pulling a function up from parsing so users can write fleetreport.load_csv instead of the longer path.

Common mistake: putting heavy or side-effecting work in __init__.py, such as opening a database connection or reading a large file. Because it runs on first import, every program that touches any part of the package pays that cost and triggers those side effects, even a quick test that needs one small helper. In a running service this shows up as slow startups and surprising failures at import time. Keep __init__.py short: simple setup and a few re-exports.

questions.prompt:
A clinic-scheduling project has app.py sitting next to a folder named clinic. That folder contains __init__.py, bookings.py and reminders.py. The only line in __init__.py prints the message "clinic ready". app.py first runs import clinic.bookings and then, on the next line, runs import clinic.reminders. Trace it.

Step 1: Python finds the folder clinic, sees __init__.py, and treats the folder as a package.
Step 2: It runs __init__.py, so "clinic ready" is printed, and it creates the package object.
Step 3: It runs the top-level code of bookings.py and attaches it as clinic.bookings.
Step 4: ???
Step 5: It runs the top-level code of reminders.py and attaches it as clinic.reminders.
Result: "clinic ready" appears exactly once in the output.

Which choice is the missing Step 4?
choices: Python sees the package clinic is already loaded and reuses that copy without running __init__.py again.
Python raises an error, because a package can only be imported once per program.
Python re-runs bookings.py together with __init__.py, because importing any module reloads every module in the package.
Python runs __init__.py a second time, because each import line starts the package load from scratch, so "clinic ready" prints again.
questions.why: A package's __init__.py runs only on the first import. Later imports reuse the copy already loaded, which is why the message prints exactly once.

questions.prompt: A folder named billing contains three files: invoice.py, tax.py and an empty __init__.py. Which statement describes this layout correctly?
choices: billing is a module, and invoice and tax are packages inside it.
billing is a package, and invoice and tax are modules within it.
billing is not a package, because its __init__.py file is empty.
billing, invoice and tax are all packages, because each one is a file or folder Python can import.
questions.why: A directory with an __init__.py is a regular package, even when that file is empty. Each .py file inside it is a module named after its filename.

questions.prompt: In a package named shop, both cart.py and checkout.py define their own function called validate. A program imports both modules. What happens to the two validate functions?
choices: Python refuses to import the second module because of the duplicate name.
The one imported second overwrites the first, so only one validate exists.
They do not clash, because each lives in its own module namespace: shop.cart.validate and shop.checkout.validate.
Both work only if one of them is renamed in __init__.py.
questions.why: Each module has its own namespace, a separate set of names, so the full names of the two functions are different and never collide.

questions.prompt: A team puts code in the __init__.py of their analytics package that downloads a 2 GB dataset. A quick unit test only needs a small rounding helper, so it runs import analytics.mathutils. What is the consequence?
choices: The download is skipped, because __init__.py only runs when the package is imported by its bare name, analytics.
The import fails at once, because __init__.py is not allowed to contain code.
The test triggers the 2 GB download, because __init__.py runs on the first import of any part of the package.
Nothing extra happens, because only mathutils.py is run when you import that one module.
questions.why: Importing any module in a package first runs the package's __init__.py, so every program that touches the package pays for the heavy work in it and triggers its side effects.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why you split the project into a folder with an __init__.py instead of keeping one big file. Explain in your own words what a module and a package are, what __init__.py does, and name one limit or tradeoff of putting code in __init__.py.
lessons.modelAnswer: A module is just one .py file, and its name is the filename. A package is a folder of related modules that Python treats as one named unit. In a regular package, the folder contains __init__.py. That file marks the folder as a package, and its code runs once, the first time anything in the package is imported. Splitting the code this way gives each file its own namespace, so names don't clash. It also makes code easy to find: parsing lives in fleetreport/parsing.py. I use __init__.py to re-export a few key functions so callers get a short path. The tradeoff is that whatever sits in __init__.py runs for anyone importing any part of the package. If I put slow or side-effecting work there, such as opening connections or reading big files, every import, even in tests, becomes slow and can fail at startup. So I keep it small.
rubricPoints: A module is a single .py file named after its filename.
A package is a directory of modules treated as one named unit, marked by __init__.py in a regular package.
__init__.py runs once on the package's first import and can be empty or re-export names.
Separate modules give separate namespaces, so names do not collide.
Heavy or side-effecting code in __init__.py slows every import and can cause failures at import time.

suggested.rationale: Laying out a small package and watching when __init__.py runs is best learned by doing, and no current mission has the learner build a multi-file package.

lessons.plain: A virtual environment is a private, self-contained folder for one project that holds its own copy of the Python setup and its own installed add-on libraries. Without one, every project on your computer shares a single pile of libraries, so upgrading something for one project can quietly break another. Think of it like giving each project its own toolbox instead of everyone grabbing from one shared garage wall. Whatever you put in one toolbox stays there, and the other projects never see it. Python ships a built-in tool called venv that creates these toolboxes for you.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have two Python projects on one laptop. One needs version 1 of a library and the other needs version 2. If both projects share the same installed libraries, what do you think goes wrong when you upgrade the library for the second project?
lessons.teach:
A virtual environment is an isolated directory containing a link to a Python interpreter (the program that runs your .py files) plus its own site-packages folder, the place where installed third-party libraries live. A dependency is any outside library your code needs to run. Dependency isolation means each project's dependencies are kept separate, so one project's choices cannot affect another's.

It works because Python decides where to look for libraries based on which interpreter is running. When you activate an environment (run a small script that adjusts your shell's PATH, the list of folders your terminal searches for commands), typing python or pip now finds the copies inside the environment folder first. Installs then land in that environment's site-packages, not the system-wide one.

Worked example. In a project folder you run python -m venv .venv, which creates a folder named .venv. Next you activate it: source .venv/bin/activate on Linux or macOS, or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows. Your prompt usually shows (.venv). Now pip install requests puts the requests library inside .venv only. Running which python (or where python on Windows) shows a path inside .venv, confirming you are isolated. In a second project you can make a different environment holding an older requests, and the two never collide. Typing deactivate returns you to the normal system Python.

A common mistake is forgetting to activate before running pip install. The library goes into the global Python instead, your project seems to work on your machine, and you do not notice it was never recorded as part of the project. Another mistake is copying or committing the .venv folder to version control; it contains machine-specific paths and should be recreated, not shared.

In a running system, skipping isolation leads to the classic "works on my laptop, fails on the server" problem, because the server lacks a library that was silently installed globally on the developer's machine.

questions.prompt: Priya is writing a small script for a veterinary clinic that sends appointment reminders. It needs an outside library called twilio. She works on macOS in a project folder named clinic-reminders and wants this dependency (an outside library her code needs) kept isolated from her other projects. Step 1: she runs python -m venv env, which creates a folder named env holding a link to a Python interpreter and its own site-packages folder. Step 2: MISSING. Step 3: her prompt now shows (env), and she runs pip install twilio, so the library lands in env's site-packages. Step 4: she runs which python and sees /Users/priya/clinic-reminders/env/bin/python, confirming she is isolated. What is Step 2?
choices: Run pip install twilio globally first so the new environment can pick up a copy of it
Run deactivate so the system Python stops interfering with the env folder
Run source env/bin/activate so the shell's PATH finds the python and pip inside env first
Commit the env folder to version control so the environment is recorded with the project
questions.why: Activating adjusts the shell's PATH so python and pip resolve to the copies inside env, which is why the prompt shows (env) and the later install and which python check point into that folder.

questions.prompt: A developer at a weather-data company activates a virtual environment before working on a forecasting tool. What does activation actually change?
choices: It temporarily uninstalls the system-wide Python until deactivate is run
It makes pip install new libraries into all of the machine's environments at once
It copies every globally installed library into the environment's site-packages
It adjusts the shell's PATH so python and pip are found inside the environment folder first
questions.why: Activation runs a small script that changes PATH, the list of folders the terminal searches for commands, so the environment's own python and pip are used and installs land in its site-packages.

questions.prompt: Marco at a logistics startup builds a route-planning script that uses a library called geopy. He has a virtual environment in his project folder but runs pip install geopy in a fresh terminal without activating it. The script runs fine on his laptop, yet on the company server it fails because geopy cannot be found. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The server's Python is too new to run any third-party library
geopy was installed into the environment, which the server cannot read
geopy went into his global Python, so it was never part of the project's environment
Virtual environments block libraries from being used on servers
questions.why: Without activation, pip resolves to the system-wide one, so the library was installed globally and silently, giving the classic works-on-my-laptop, fails-on-the-server problem.

questions.prompt: A design agency has two projects on one laptop: a thumbnail generator that needs an older version of an image library, and a new gallery app that needs the latest version. What approach keeps both working without conflict?
choices: Create a separate virtual environment for each project and install the needed version in each
Create one environment for the thumbnail project and copy its folder into the gallery project
Install both versions into the system-wide Python and let Python pick one
Install only the latest version globally, since newer versions always support old code
questions.why: Each virtual environment has its own site-packages, so dependency isolation lets each project hold its own library version without the two ever colliding.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never used one why each Python project should have its own virtual environment, how you create and use one, and name at least one limit or tradeoff of virtual environments.
lessons.modelAnswer: A virtual environment is a per-project folder with its own pointer to a Python interpreter and its own site-packages, where installed libraries go. You create it with python -m venv .venv and activate it, which puts that folder first on your PATH, so python and pip refer to the environment's copies. Anything you pip install then stays inside that project, so two projects can use different versions of the same library without breaking each other. Always check the prompt or run which python before installing, or you will install globally by accident. The limits: an environment does not isolate the Python version itself beyond the interpreter it was built from, nor system-level things like C libraries. It also costs disk space per project, and the folder is not portable, so you share a list of dependencies and rebuild it rather than copying .venv around.
rubricPoints: Defines a virtual environment as an isolated folder with its own interpreter link and installed libraries.
Explains that activation changes which python and pip are found, so installs land in the environment.
States the benefit: different projects can use conflicting library versions safely.
Mentions the risk of installing without activating, causing hidden global dependencies.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as no isolation of system libraries, disk use, or the folder not being portable.

suggested.rationale: No current mission has the learner create and activate an environment, and a hands-on Python drill where they build one, install a library and verify isolation is the most direct way to learn it.

lessons.plain: Most Python projects lean on code written by other people, called dependencies. pip is the tool that downloads and installs that code for you, usually from PyPI, the public online catalogue of Python libraries. Pinning means writing down the exact version of each dependency you used, so everyone gets the same thing. The usual place to write it is a plain text file called requirements.txt. Think of a recipe that says "2 cups of Brand X flour, 2023 batch" instead of just "flour". Anyone following it bakes the same cake, not a slightly different one.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your project works today with a library at version 2.31. Six months from now, a new teammate installs "the latest" version of that library instead. What could go wrong, and how might you prevent it?
lessons.teach:
pip is Python's package installer. It fetches a distributed library from PyPI (the Python Package Index, the public online library catalogue) and installs it into the active Python environment. A dependency is any outside library your code needs. A transitive dependency is a library that one of your dependencies needs in turn.

A version specifier tells pip which versions are acceptable. "requests" alone means any version, so you get the newest. "requests>=2.28" sets a minimum. "requests==2.31.0" is a pin: exactly that version and nothing else. Pinning works because published versions on PyPI do not change. So the same pins always rebuild the same set of code.

requirements.txt is a text file with one specifier per line. "pip freeze" prints every installed package with its exact version, in that same format. "pip install -r requirements.txt" installs everything the file lists.

Worked example. Step 1: inside your project's virtual environment, run "pip install requests==2.31.0". Step 2: pip also installs requests' own needs, such as urllib3, idna, certifi and charset-normalizer. Step 3: run "pip freeze > requirements.txt". The file now pins all five packages, transitive ones included. Step 4: commit the file. Step 5: a teammate creates a fresh environment and runs "pip install -r requirements.txt". They get identical versions.

Common mistake: running pip freeze outside a virtual environment. That dumps every package ever installed on the machine into the file, including unrelated tools. A related slip is running a pip that belongs to a different Python than the one you run your code with. Using "python -m pip" avoids that.

The tradeoff: pins do not update themselves. You must deliberately upgrade them to pick up security fixes. Without pins, a running system can break the next time it is rebuilt or deployed, because a new upstream release slipped in with nobody changing a line of your code.

questions.prompt:
A volunteer at an animal shelter writes a Python script that uses the pandas library. The volunteer wants anyone who sets the script up later to get exactly the same versions of every library. Here is the process, with one step missing.

Step 1: Activate the script's own virtual environment (an isolated Python setup used only for this project).
Step 2: Run "python -m pip install pandas==2.1.4". pip also installs the other libraries pandas needs, such as numpy. These are transitive dependencies (libraries your dependency needs in turn).
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Commit the resulting requirements.txt file to the shared repository.
Step 5: On a new laptop, someone creates a fresh virtual environment and runs "python -m pip install -r requirements.txt". They get identical versions.

What is Step 3?
choices: Run "pip freeze > requirements.txt" from a terminal where no virtual environment is active
Open requirements.txt and type "pandas>=2.1" so that newer fixes are picked up automatically
Open requirements.txt and type the single line "pandas", because pip will work out the rest
Still inside the activated virtual environment, run "pip freeze > requirements.txt"
questions.why: Running pip freeze inside the project's environment writes an exact pin for every installed package, including transitive ones like numpy, and lists nothing unrelated, so a rebuild gets identical versions.

questions.prompt: A version specifier tells pip which versions of a library are acceptable. Which line in a requirements.txt file is a pin, meaning exactly one version is allowed and nothing else?
choices: numpy
numpy>=1.0
questions.why: The double equals sign accepts exactly that one version. A bare name accepts any version, and >= only sets a minimum.

questions.prompt: A delivery company's tracking service lists its dependencies in requirements.txt with no version numbers, only library names. Last month it deployed fine. Today the team redeploys the same code without changing a single line, and the service crashes on startup. What is the most likely cause?
choices: pip freeze was run inside a virtual environment, which removed the transitive dependencies from the file
With no pins, the rebuild installed a newer upstream release of a library, and that release behaves differently
Unpinned files force pip to install the oldest available version of each library
Published versions on PyPI were edited after release, so last month's version now contains different code
questions.why: Without pins, pip installs the newest versions, so a new upstream release can slip in at rebuild time with no change to your own code. Published versions on PyPI do not change, which is why pins give repeatable builds.

questions.prompt: A developer at a small accounting firm runs "pip freeze > requirements.txt" for a tiny invoice tool that uses only one outside library. The file ends up with over 80 lines, including code formatters and tools from unrelated old projects. What most likely went wrong?
choices: They forgot to pin the one library, so pip freeze added alternatives just in case
pip freeze always lists every transitive dependency of every package on PyPI
They ran pip freeze outside the project's virtual environment, so it listed every package installed on the machine
They used "python -m pip" instead of plain "pip", which widens what gets listed
questions.why: pip freeze lists everything installed in the active environment. Outside a virtual environment, that means every package on the machine, including unrelated tools.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the project keeps a pinned requirements.txt and how they should use it. Include one limit or tradeoff of pinning.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our code depends on outside libraries that pip installs from PyPI. If we only wrote "requests", everyone would get whatever version was newest on the day they installed. Then a new release could quietly break the build or production even though our code never changed. So we pin exact versions with == in requirements.txt. We generate it with pip freeze from inside the project's virtual environment, so it captures our libraries and their transitive dependencies, and nothing else from the machine.
