To set up, make a fresh venv and run python -m pip install -r requirements.txt, and you'll match everyone else. The tradeoff is that pins freeze us in time. We won't get bug or security fixes automatically, so someone has to upgrade the pins on purpose, test, and commit the new file.
rubricPoints: pip installs libraries from PyPI into the active environment.
Pinning with == fixes an exact version so installs are reproducible.
requirements.txt lists the specifiers and is installed with pip install -r.
pip freeze should be run inside the project's virtual environment so it captures transitive dependencies without unrelated packages.
Unpinned dependencies can break a build or deploy when a new upstream release appears.
Tradeoff: pins must be upgraded deliberately to get security and bug fixes.

suggested.rationale: Installing, freezing and reinstalling from a pinned file is a hands-on habit best built by actually running the steps in a guided Python drill.

lessons.plain: Python comes with a large built-in toolbox called the standard library. It is a set of ready-made modules (files of code) that you can load with one import line and nothing extra to install. Five of them show up in almost every practical script. os talks to the operating system. sys talks to the running Python program itself. datetime does date and time arithmetic. collections offers smarter containers such as counters. itertools gives tools for working through sequences efficiently. Think of it as the drawer of tools that came with the house: check there before you buy anything new.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a list of HTTP status codes from a log, such as 500, 404, 500, 200, 500. Without writing a loop yourself, what kind of ready-made tool would you hope Python already provides to tell you which code appears most often?
lessons.teach:
The standard library is the set of modules that ships with every Python install. A module is a file of Python code that you load with import. You can use all of these without installing anything. Five of them are worth knowing early.

os talks to the operating system. os.environ is a dictionary-like view of environment variables, which are named settings the shell passes to a program. os.path.join builds file paths using the correct separator for the system.

sys talks to the running Python interpreter. sys.argv is the list of command-line arguments. sys.exit(1) stops the program with a non-zero exit code, and that code tells the shell or a CI job that something failed.

datetime handles dates and times. A timedelta is a length of time that you can add to or subtract from a date.

collections offers specialised containers. Counter counts things. defaultdict fills in a default value when a key is missing. deque is a queue that is fast to add to and remove from at both ends.

itertools works with iterators. An iterator is an object that hands out items one at a time, on demand, without building the whole list in memory. Two useful tools are islice, which takes the first n items, and groupby, which bundles neighbouring items that share a key.

Worked example: count error codes from the last hour. It is now 11:00, so cutoff = datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=1) gives 10:00. The log has three lines: 10:05 code 500, 10:40 code 404, and 10:50 code 500. All three are after 10:00, so all of them pass the filter. Feed the codes to Counter: 500 becomes 1, then 404 becomes 1, then 500 becomes 2. most_common(1) returns [(500, 2)]. If that count is over a threshold, sys.exit(1) signals failure.

A common mistake is using groupby on unsorted data. It only groups adjacent items, so 500, 404, 500 produces three groups, not two. Sort by the same key first. In a running system this does not crash anything. It quietly produces wrong reports or missed alerts, which makes it hard to spot.

questions.prompt: A warehouse logs the zone of each pallet it scans during a shift: B, A, B, C, A. The supervisor wants one group per zone with a count, using itertools.groupby (a tool that bundles neighbouring items sharing the same key). Step 1: collect the zone letters into a list: [B, A, B, C, A]. Step 2: ??? Step 3: run groupby over the result and count each group, giving A: 2, B: 2, C: 1. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Wrap the list in islice(zones, 5) so groupby receives exactly five items
Leave the list as it is, because groupby gathers every matching letter wherever it appears
Sort the list by zone so that matching letters sit next to each other
Load the list into a deque so groupby can read it quickly from both ends
questions.why: groupby only bundles adjacent items, so sorting by zone first places both A's together and both B's together, which gives one group per zone.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm deploys a script that must read a secret key. The shell supplies the key as a named setting called API_TOKEN. Which standard library feature should the script use to read it?
choices: collections.defaultdict, which fills in a value when a key is missing
os.environ, the dictionary-like view of environment variables
sys.argv, the list of command-line arguments
os.path.join, which builds file paths with the right separator
questions.why: Named settings that the shell passes to a program are environment variables, and os.environ is how Python reads them.

questions.prompt: A community library records that a member borrowed a book on 3 March. Its system calculates the due date as borrowed_date + timedelta(days=14). What due date does this produce?
choices: 3 April
16 March
14 March
17 March
questions.why: A timedelta is a length of time added to a date, so 3 March plus 14 days is 17 March.

questions.prompt: A team's CI job runs a validation script. When the script finds a broken config file, it prints "config invalid" and then reaches the end normally without calling sys.exit(1). What is the most likely result?
choices: The CI job reports success, because the program never signalled failure with a non-zero exit code
Python raises an error automatically, because any script that prints a warning has to call sys.exit
The CI job pauses and waits for a person to read the message before it continues
The CI job fails, because the printed message tells CI that something went wrong
questions.why: The shell and CI learn about failure from a non-zero exit code, such as the one sys.exit(1) sets, not from printed text, so a script that ends normally looks like a success.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what os, sys, datetime, collections and itertools are each for, and name one limit or trap to watch for when using them.
lessons.modelAnswer: These are standard library modules, so they ship with Python and need no installing. os is for dealing with the operating system, for example reading environment variables or building file paths that work on any platform. sys is about the interpreter itself: command-line arguments in sys.argv, and sys.exit with a non-zero code to tell a shell or CI job we failed. datetime does date maths, such as subtracting a timedelta of one hour to get a cutoff. collections gives better containers. Counter tallies items and can return the most common ones, and defaultdict avoids missing-key errors. itertools works lazily on iterators, so we can handle big inputs without loading everything into memory. One trap is that itertools.groupby only groups neighbouring items. If you forget to sort first, you get split groups and wrong counts. The script does not crash, so it fails quietly.
rubricPoints: States that these modules ship with Python and need no installation.
Gives a correct purpose for os (operating system) and sys (interpreter, argv, exit codes).
Describes datetime with timedelta arithmetic and collections with an example such as Counter.
Explains that itertools works lazily on iterators, saving memory.
Names a real trap, such as groupby needing sorted input, and its quiet consequence.

suggested.rationale: Short hands-on drills that make the learner reach for Counter, timedelta, sys.exit and groupby fit this broad module tour better than any single existing mission.

lessons.plain: An iterator is an object that hands you items one at a time, on request, and remembers where it is. Think of a ticket dispenser at a deli counter. You pull, you get the next number, and the machine keeps track of what comes after. When the roll runs out, it tells you it is empty. A for loop in Python is someone pulling that ticket over and over until the dispenser says it is done. Because only one item exists at a time, you can walk through huge or endless streams of data without holding all of it in memory.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you loop over the same open file twice in a row with two for loops, what do you think the second loop prints, and why?
lessons.teach:
An iterable is anything you can loop over, such as a list, a string or an open file. An iterator is the object that does the actual stepping through. The iterator protocol is the agreement between the two, and it has two special methods. __iter__ returns an iterator. __next__ returns the next item, or raises StopIteration, a built-in exception that means there are no more items. The built-in functions iter(x) and next(it) call those two methods for you.

A for loop runs this protocol behind the scenes. It calls iter() once on the thing you gave it, then calls next() repeatedly, and it stops quietly when StopIteration is raised.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a Countdown class stores self.n = 3. Its __iter__ returns self, and its __next__ checks whether n is 0. If it is, it raises StopIteration. Otherwise it saves n, subtracts 1, and returns the saved value. Now trace for x in Countdown(3). First, iter() returns the object itself. The first next() returns 3 and n becomes 2. The next call returns 2, then 1. On the fourth call n is 0, so StopIteration is raised and the loop ends. Only one number existed at any moment.

A common mistake is to forget that an iterator is used up once it runs out. Countdown returns itself from __iter__, so looping over the same Countdown object a second time produces nothing, because n is already 0. Files and map objects behave the same way. Lists are different: each call to iter() on a list creates a fresh iterator, so a list can be looped over many times. To make a class reusable, have its __iter__ build and return a new iterator object each time.

In a running system, this mistake shows up as a silent bug. A report that loops over the same stream twice gets an empty result on the second pass and raises no error. The payoff is memory. An iterator over a 50 GB log file holds only one line at a time.

questions.prompt: A bakery app has an OrderQueue class that stores self.orders = ["bagel", "scone"] and a position counter self.i = 0. Its __iter__ returns self. Its __next__ first checks whether i equals the number of orders. If it does, it raises StopIteration. Otherwise it saves the order at position i, adds 1 to i, and returns the saved order. The code runs q = OrderQueue(), then it = iter(q), then calls next(it) three times. Step 1: iter(q) calls __iter__, which returns q itself. Step 2: the first next(it) returns "bagel", and i becomes 1. Step 3: the second next(it) returns "scone", and i becomes 2. Step 4 is missing. What happens on the third call to next(it)?
choices: It returns None, because there are no orders left to give back.
It returns "bagel" again, because the iterator starts over from the first order.
It returns "scone" again, because i stays at the last valid position.
It raises StopIteration, because i now equals 2, the number of orders.
questions.why: After two orders, i equals the number of orders, so __next__ raises StopIteration to signal that no items remain; iterators never restart or return None on their own.

questions.prompt: In Python's iterator protocol, which special method hands back the next item, or raises StopIteration when nothing is left?
choices: __len__
__getitem__
__iter__
__next__
questions.why: __next__ produces each item in turn and raises StopIteration at the end, while __iter__ only returns the iterator object.

questions.prompt: A payroll script sets rows = map(parse, lines). It loops over rows once to add up the total pay. Then it loops over the same rows object again to count the employees. What happens in the second loop?
choices: It raises a TypeError, because a map object cannot be used in a for loop.
It runs zero times without any error, so the employee count silently comes out as 0.
It loops over every row again, because map remembers its results like a list.
It raises StopIteration as an error, and the script crashes with a traceback.
questions.why: A map object is an iterator that is used up after one pass, and a for loop treats StopIteration as a quiet stop, so the second loop does nothing and raises no error.

questions.prompt: A music app has a Playlist class whose __iter__ returns self and whose __next__ steps through the songs. Users report that playing the playlist a second time does nothing. What change lets the same Playlist object be looped over many times?
choices: Make __iter__ build and return a new iterator object each time it is called.
Add a __len__ method so Python knows how many songs exist.
Make __next__ raise StopIteration one item earlier.
Call next() on the playlist twice before each loop starts.
questions.why: A for loop calls iter() at the start of every loop, so returning a fresh iterator each time gives every loop its own starting position, just as a list does.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what actually happens when Python runs a for loop over an object, and name one limitation of iterators they must watch out for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A for loop first calls iter() on the object, which calls its __iter__ method and gets back an iterator. Then it calls next() on that iterator over and over. Each call runs __next__, which returns one item and moves the position forward. When there is nothing left, __next__ raises StopIteration, and the loop catches that and ends quietly. Because items are produced one at a time, we can process a huge file without loading it all into memory. The limitation is that an iterator is single-use. Once it is exhausted, looping over it again gives nothing and raises no error, which is easy to miss in a report that loops twice. You also can't index into it or ask for its length. If you need several passes, either make __iter__ return a new iterator each time, the way lists do, or reopen or recreate the source.
rubricPoints: States that a for loop calls iter() once and then next() repeatedly.
Explains that __next__ returns one item at a time and raises StopIteration when finished.
Distinguishes an iterable from an iterator.
Names exhaustion or single use as a limit, and notes that it fails silently.
Connects one-at-a-time production to low memory use on large data.

suggested.rationale: Writing a small class with __iter__ and __next__, then seeing it run out on a second loop, is best learned by running Python drills, and no current mission focuses on the iterator protocol.

lessons.plain: A generator is a function that hands you results one at a time, only when you ask for the next one, instead of building the whole pile up front. Think of a tap rather than a bucket: a bucket must be filled completely before you carry it, while a tap gives you water as you need it and never holds more than a little. In Python, the word yield marks the spot where the function hands over one value and pauses. A generator expression is a one-line shorthand for the same idea. Because only one item exists at a time, generators can process huge files without running out of memory.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a function hands back one value and then pauses instead of finishing, what do you think happens to its local variables while it waits for you to ask for the next value?
lessons.teach:
A generator function is an ordinary-looking function that contains the keyword yield. Calling it does not run the body. Instead it returns a generator object, which is an iterator: something you can ask for one value at a time, using next() or a for loop. Each time a value is requested, the body runs until it reaches yield. It hands that value back and pauses, with all its local variables kept intact. The next request resumes right after the yield. When the body finishes, the generator raises StopIteration, the signal a for loop uses to stop.

This works because values are produced lazily, meaning only when asked for. Only the current item lives in memory, so a generator can walk a 50 GB log file or even an endless sequence.

Worked example: def evens(limit): n = 0; while n < limit: yield n; n += 2. Calling g = evens(5) runs nothing yet. The first next(g) starts the body, sets n to 0, yields 0, and pauses. The second next(g) resumes, makes n 2, passes the loop check, and yields 2. The third makes n 4 and yields 4. The fourth makes n 6, so the loop ends and the body finishes, raising StopIteration.

A generator expression is the compact form. (line.strip() for line in f if line) looks like a list comprehension but uses parentheses, so it builds a generator instead of a full list. You can chain them into a pipeline: errors = (l for l in open('app.log') if 'ERROR' in l), then count = sum(1 for _ in errors). Each stage pulls one line from the stage before it, so the whole file is never held at once.

Common mistake: reusing a generator. It is single-use, so once exhausted, a second loop over it silently yields nothing. If you need two passes, create a new generator or deliberately store a list. The opposite mistake also hurts a running system. Writing square brackets instead of parentheses on a huge input loads everything into memory, which can get the process killed for running out of RAM.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain tracks how its order batches grow. A developer writes: def batches(cap): k = 1; while k < cap: yield k; k *= 3. Then g = batches(20). Trace so far: creating g runs nothing. The first next(g) starts the body, sets k to 1, passes the check 1 < 20, yields 1, and pauses. The second next(g) resumes, makes k 3, passes the check, and yields 3. The third next(g) makes k 9, passes the check, and yields 9. What happens on the fourth next(g)?
choices: It makes k 27 and yields 27, because a value is always produced before the check runs again.
It starts the body over from the top, sets k back to 1, and yields 1 again.
It makes k 27, the check 27 < 20 fails, the body finishes, and the generator raises StopIteration.
It returns 9 again, because the paused generator keeps handing back its last yielded value.
questions.why: Execution resumes right after the yield, so k becomes 27, the loop condition fails, and a finished body raises StopIteration.

questions.prompt: A developer at a shipping firm defines a function containing the keyword yield and then writes r = routes(). What has that line done?
choices: It ran the whole body and stored every yielded value in a list called r.
It raised StopIteration, because no for loop is asking for values.
It ran the body up to the first yield and stored that first value in r.
It returned a generator object without running any of the function body yet.
questions.why: Calling a generator function only creates a generator object; the body runs only when a value is requested with next() or a for loop.

questions.prompt: A wind-farm team has a 40 GB file of turbine readings, turbines.csv, and wants to count lines containing 'FAULT' on a machine with 8 GB of RAM. Which code does this while holding only about one line in memory at a time?
choices: faults = [l for l in open('turbines.csv') if 'FAULT' in l]; n = len(faults)
n = sum([1 for l in open('turbines.csv') if 'FAULT' in l])
faults = (l for l in open('turbines.csv') if 'FAULT' in l); n = sum(1 for _ in faults)
n = len(list(l for l in open('turbines.csv') if 'FAULT' in l))
questions.why: Parentheses build generators that pull one line at a time, while square brackets or list() build a full list in memory first.

questions.prompt: At a clinic, a developer writes temps = (t for t in readings if t > 38.0), then total = sum(temps), then count = sum(1 for _ in temps). The total is correct but count is always 0. Why?
choices: The generator was used up by the first sum(), and an exhausted generator silently yields nothing on a second pass.
sum() converts the generator into a list and then deletes it, leaving temps empty.
A generator expression cannot be passed to sum() more than once without raising an error.
The condition t > 38.0 is checked only once, so the second pass filters out every value.
questions.why: Generators are single-use, so the second loop gets nothing; making a new generator or deliberately storing a list fixes it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what yield does and why a generator pipeline is better than building lists when processing a large log file. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of using generators.
lessons.modelAnswer: A function with yield becomes a generator. Calling it doesn't run the code. It gives you an object you pull values from with next() or a for loop. Each pull runs the body up to the next yield, hands that value out, and pauses with its local state saved. When the body ends, StopIteration tells the loop to stop. Because values are made lazily, only one item is in memory at a time. So I can chain generator expressions, like reading lines, then filtering errors, then counting, and memory stays flat no matter how big the file is. A list version would load every line first and could crash on a huge file. The tradeoffs: a generator is single-use, so a second loop gets nothing. It also has no length or indexing. If I need multiple passes or random access, I should store a list on purpose.
rubricPoints: Calling a generator function returns a generator object without running the body.
yield hands back one value and pauses, keeping local variables for the next request.
Values are produced lazily, so memory use stays small even for huge inputs.
A generator expression uses parentheses and builds a generator, not a list.
Chained generators form a pipeline where each stage pulls one item at a time.
Limit: generators are single-use, with no length or indexing, so a second pass needs a new generator or a stored list.

suggested.rationale: Tracing when a generator pauses and resumes, and rewriting list-based code as a pipeline, is best learned by running small drills, and no current mission requires generators.

lessons.plain: In Python, a function is a value, just like a number or a piece of text. You can store it in a variable, put it in a list, or hand it to another function so that function can use it later. Think of giving a coworker a sorting rule written on a card instead of sorting the pile yourself: they do the sorting, and your card tells them how to compare things. A lambda is a quick way to write a tiny, unnamed function on the spot, the way you might scribble a rule on a sticky note instead of filing a formal document.
lessons.guessPrompt: Python's sorted function can take an extra rule that tells it what to compare. If you have the words ['pear', 'fig', 'banana'] and you hand sorted the built-in len function as that rule, what order do you think comes back, and why?
lessons.teach:
A first-class function is a function the language treats as an ordinary value: you can assign it to a variable, store it in a data structure, return it, and pass it as an argument (an input given to another function). A function that receives another function and calls it is often called a higher-order function, and the function passed in is often called a callback.

This works because the function's name refers to a function object. Writing len with no parentheses refers to that object; writing len(x) runs it. The receiving function decides when, and on what, to run it.

A lambda expression creates a small function without a name: lambda x: x * 2 takes one input x and returns x * 2. Its body must be a single expression; it cannot hold statements such as loops or assignments.

Worked example: sorted(['pear', 'fig', 'banana'], key=len). Here key is a parameter expecting a key function, which sorted calls once per item to get a value to compare. Step one: sorted calls len('pear') giving 4, len('fig') giving 3, len('banana') giving 6. Step two: it orders items by those numbers: 3, 4, 6. Result: ['fig', 'pear', 'banana']. With a lambda, key=lambda w: w[-1] sorts by last letter: 'banana' (a), 'pear' (r), 'fig' (g)... ordered a, g, r gives ['banana', 'fig', 'pear'].

Common mistake: adding parentheses, as in key=len(). That calls len immediately with nothing and fails, and in other cases calling a function early passes its result instead of the function itself. Pass the name, not a call. In a running system, this mistake in a callback for retries or event handling means the code runs once at setup rather than when the event happens, a bug that can hide until production.

Use lambdas for short throwaway rules; once logic grows or needs reuse, define a named function with def, because named functions read better and show their name in error tracebacks.

questions.prompt: A warehouse script sorts temperature readings by how far each one is from zero: sorted([-7, 2, -3], key=abs). Here abs is a built-in function that returns a number's distance from zero, and it is passed by name, without parentheses, as the key function. Step one is missing. Step two: sorted orders the readings by the numbers it got in step one, smallest first: 2, 3, 7. Result: [2, -3, -7]. What happens in step one?
choices: sorted compares -7, 2 and -3 directly as they are, and abs is only applied to the finished list.
sorted calls abs once on the whole list [-7, 2, -3] and gets back one number to sort by.
sorted calls abs once per reading: abs(-7) gives 7, abs(2) gives 2, and abs(-3) gives 3.
sorted calls abs() once with no input before sorting begins, and uses that single result for every reading.
questions.why: A key function is called once per item to produce the value that gets compared, so abs runs on -7, 2 and -3 separately, giving 7, 2 and 3.

questions.prompt: A library app has a function apply_discount(price, rule) that calls rule(price) inside its body. A developer calls it as apply_discount(40, half_off), where half_off is a function. Which description fits this code?
choices: half_off is a higher-order function, and apply_discount is its callback.
apply_discount is a higher-order function, and half_off is a callback passed to it.
half_off runs immediately when the line is read, and apply_discount receives its result.
Both are lambda expressions, because one of them is passed as an argument.
questions.why: A function that receives another function and calls it is a higher-order function, and the function passed in, here half_off named without parentheses, is the callback.

questions.prompt: A café sorts drink names by their second letter: sorted(['tea', 'espresso', 'mocha'], key=lambda d: d[1]). The second letters are 'e' for tea, 's' for espresso and 'o' for mocha. What is the result?
choices: ['tea', 'espresso', 'mocha'], because a lambda cannot be used as a key
['tea', 'mocha', 'espresso'], because the key letters e, o, s are put in order
['espresso', 'mocha', 'tea'], because the lambda sorts by the first letter
['mocha', 'tea', 'espresso'], because the lambda sorts by the last letter
questions.why: sorted calls the lambda once per name to get 'e', 's' and 'o', then orders the names by those letters: e, o, s.

questions.prompt: A delivery company registers a function to run each time a parcel scan fails: scanner.on_failure(handler=notify_driver()). In testing, a driver gets one message the moment the program starts, and no messages when real scans fail. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The parentheses call notify_driver once at setup and pass its result, so the function itself is never registered to run on failure.
The handler argument only accepts functions whose bodies are a single expression, so notify_driver is silently ignored.
Passing a function by name always runs it once immediately and then again on every later failure event.
notify_driver should have been written as a lambda, because a named function made with def cannot be passed as an argument.
questions.why: Writing notify_driver() runs the function right away and hands over its result, so the callback fires once at setup instead of when failures happen; passing notify_driver without parentheses fixes it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what it means that Python functions are first-class, how passing a function or a lambda to something like sorted works, and name one limit or tradeoff of using lambdas.
lessons.modelAnswer: In Python a function is just an object, so I can store it in a variable or pass it into another function, which then calls it when it needs to. For example, sorted takes a key argument: I hand it a function, and sorted calls it on every item and orders the items by whatever that function returns. Passing len sorts words by length. The important detail is passing the name without parentheses; writing len() would call it immediately instead of handing it over. A lambda is a shorthand for a small nameless function, like lambda w: w[-1] to sort by last letter. The tradeoff is that a lambda can only be one expression, has no meaningful name in error tracebacks, and becomes hard to read if it grows. For anything longer or reused, I would write a named function with def instead.
rubricPoints: States that functions are values that can be stored and passed as arguments.
Explains that the receiving function calls the passed function itself, e.g. sorted calling a key function per item.
Distinguishes passing a function name from calling it with parentheses.
Defines a lambda as a small anonymous single-expression function.
Names a lambda limit such as single-expression only, no name in tracebacks, or reduced readability.

suggested.rationale: Short hands-on drills where the learner passes key functions and lambdas and sees the results would build this skill best, and no current mission focuses on it.

lessons.plain: Python has a few small tools for processing a collection of things in steps. One applies the same change to every item (map). One keeps only the items that pass a test (filter). One squashes a whole collection down to a single answer, such as a total (reduce). A standard toolbox module called itertools adds more ready-made parts: taking the first few items, joining sequences, grouping neighbours. Think of a factory conveyor belt: one station paints every part, one rejects faulty parts, and one packs everything into a single box. Items move one at a time, so the belt never needs room for the whole batch at once.
lessons.guessPrompt: You apply a 'double it' step to each of the numbers 1, 2 and 3, then keep only the results greater than 3. Which numbers are left at the end?
lessons.teach:
map(function, iterable) applies a function to every item and hands back the results one at a time. filter(function, iterable) keeps only the items for which the function returns a truthy value, meaning True or anything Python treats as true. functools.reduce(function, iterable, start) folds a sequence into one value: it calls the function on a running total and the next item, over and over. An iterable is anything you can loop over. map and filter return lazy iterators: objects that compute the next value only when asked, so nothing is calculated or stored ahead of time. The itertools module adds lazy building blocks: islice takes a slice of any iterator without building a list, chain joins iterables end to end, takewhile yields items until a condition first fails, and groupby bundles neighbouring items that share a key.

Worked example: total bytes of successful requests, where records = [("200", 512), ("500", 0), ("200", 300)].
Step 1: ok = filter(lambda r: r[0] == "200", records). A lambda is a small unnamed one-line function. Nothing runs yet.
Step 2: sizes = map(lambda r: r[1], ok). Still nothing runs.
Step 3: total = reduce(lambda acc, s: acc + s, sizes, 0). Now reduce pulls items. The first record passes the filter, map yields 512, acc becomes 512. The second fails and is skipped. The third yields 300, acc becomes 812. Result: 812.

Common mistake: reusing a map or filter result. An iterator is used up after one pass, so looping over sizes a second time silently gives nothing. Convert it to a list only if you truly need it twice. Likewise, groupby only groups adjacent items, so sort by the key first.

In a running system this laziness is the point: a chained pipeline over a 50 GB log reads one line at a time, so memory stays flat instead of growing with the file. For simple totals the built-in sum is clearer than reduce.

questions.prompt: A community library tracks overdue fines in pounds per member: fines = [0, 2, 0, 5, 3]. Staff want the total owed in pence, counting only members who owe something. The pipeline: Step 1: owed = filter(lambda f: f > 0, fines). Nothing runs yet. Step 2: pence = map(lambda f: f * 100, owed). Still nothing runs. Step 3: total = reduce(lambda acc, p: acc + p, pence, 0). Now reduce pulls items. The first 0 fails the filter and is skipped. The 2 passes, map yields 200, and acc becomes 200. The second 0 is skipped. The 5 passes and map yields 500. [MISSING STEP: what is acc now?] The 3 passes, map yields 300, and acc becomes 1000. What belongs in the missing step?
choices: acc becomes 500, because reduce replaces the running total with each new item
Nothing is added yet, because reduce waits until every item has been stored in a list
acc becomes 700, because reduce adds the new item 500 to the running total of 200
acc becomes 205, because map has not converted the 5 into pence yet
questions.why: reduce calls the function on the running total (200) and the next item that map yields (500), so acc becomes 700, which leads to the final 1000.

questions.prompt: A warehouse script groups shelf codes with itertools.groupby. groupby bundles neighbouring items that share a key. The script runs groupby on the list ["A", "A", "B", "A"] using each code as its own key, without sorting the list first. What groups does it produce?
choices: Three groups: A with two items, then B with one item, then A with one item
Two groups: A with three items and B with one item
One group containing all four items
Two groups: A with two items and B with two items
questions.why: groupby only bundles adjacent items, so the final A starts a new group. You would sort by the key first to get a single A group.

questions.prompt: A ticketing system builds evens = filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, [4, 7, 10]). It then prints list(evens) once, and on the next line prints list(evens) again. What does the second print show?
choices: [4, 7, 10], because the second pass ignores the filter function
[], because the iterator was used up by the first pass
[4, 10], because filter keeps its results stored for later use
An error, because a filter result can never be converted to a list
questions.why: filter returns a lazy iterator, which is used up after one pass, so looping over it a second time silently gives nothing.

questions.prompt: A weather station sends depth readings in the order [4, 9, -1, 6]. The code is itertools.takewhile(lambda x: x >= 0, readings). takewhile yields items until a condition first fails. Which values does it yield?
choices: 4, 9 and 6
Only -1
4 and 9
questions.why: takewhile stops for good at the first item that fails the condition (-1), so the later 6 is never reached.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what map, filter, reduce and a couple of itertools functions do, and why chaining them can process a huge file without running out of memory. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of this style.
lessons.modelAnswer: map runs a function on every item, filter keeps only items that pass a test, and functools.reduce folds everything into one value by repeatedly combining a running result with the next item. From itertools, islice grabs part of a stream without building a list, chain joins streams, and groupby bundles neighbouring items with the same key. map, filter and the itertools tools are lazy: they produce one value at a time only when the next step asks. So if I chain them over a big log, only one line is in memory at any moment, and memory stays flat no matter how large the file is. The tradeoffs: an iterator can only be consumed once, so a second loop silently gets nothing; groupby needs sorted input or it splits groups; and reduce with a lambda is often harder to read than a built-in like sum or a plain loop.
rubricPoints: States that map transforms every item and filter keeps items passing a test.
States that reduce combines items into a single value using a running result.
Names at least one itertools function and what it does.
Explains that map, filter and itertools are lazy, producing one item at a time, which keeps memory flat.
Names a limit such as single-use iterators, groupby needing sorted input, or reduce hurting readability.

suggested.rationale: These functions are best learned by writing and running small pipelines and seeing laziness and exhaustion for yourself, which a Python drills engine would provide and no current mission targets directly.

lessons.plain: A closure is a function that remembers variables from the place where it was created, even after that place has finished running. Picture a note pinned to a shared whiteboard rather than a photo of it: the function does not keep a snapshot of the values. It keeps a link to the variables themselves, so it reads whatever they hold at the moment it runs. This is what lets you build small, self-contained helpers such as counters or customised formatters. It also explains a classic surprise, where several functions made in a loop all end up seeing the same final value.
lessons.guessPrompt: You make three small functions in a loop that runs with i equal to 0, then 1, then 2. Each function just returns i. After the loop ends, you call all three. What do you expect them to return, and why?
lessons.teach:
A closure is a function that remembers variables from the function it was defined inside, even after that outer function has returned. Those remembered names are called free variables: names the inner function uses but does not assign itself. Python stores each one in a small shared container called a cell, which both the outer function and the inner function point to.

Why it works: when the outer function returns the inner one, Python attaches those cells to it. You can inspect them as fn.__closure__. The key fact is that a closure captures the variable, not the value the variable had when the function was defined. Each time the inner function runs, it looks up the current value in the cell. This is called late binding.

Worked example: a loop runs for i in range(3) and appends lambda: i to a list. Step 1: the loop uses a single variable i in the enclosing scope. Step 2: each lambda captures that same i, not a copy of it. Step 3: the loop finishes with i equal to 2. Step 4: calling each lambda reads i now, so all three return 2, not 0, 1 and 2.

There are two fixes. First, write lambda i=i: i. Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so each lambda stores its own value. Second, build each function from a factory function that takes i as a parameter. Every call to the factory creates a fresh cell, so each closure gets its own.

A related rule covers changing a captured variable. Reading it is fine. Assigning to it inside the inner function, as in count += 1, makes Python treat the name as a new local variable. If that local is read before it is assigned, Python raises UnboundLocalError. Declare the name nonlocal to rebind the outer variable instead.

The common mistake is assuming a closure takes a snapshot of values. In a running system this shows up as callbacks created in a loop that all act on the last item, such as every scheduled job processing the final file. Closures also keep captured objects alive for as long as the function exists, so capturing a large list holds onto its memory.

questions.prompt: A cinema's booking app builds one button handler per seat. The code runs: for seat in ["A1", "B2", "C3"]: handlers.append(lambda: "reserve " + seat). Trace it. Step 1: the loop uses a single variable named seat in the enclosing scope. Step 2: each lambda captures that same seat variable, not a copy of its value. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: calling handlers[0]() returns "reserve C3", and so do the other two handlers. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Python raises UnboundLocalError because seat is read inside the lambda before it is assigned there.
Each lambda stores the value seat had at the moment it was created, so the first one keeps "A1".
Python deletes seat when the loop ends, so each lambda falls back to the last string it saw.
The loop finishes with seat equal to "C3", and each lambda looks up seat's current value when it is called.
questions.why: Closures use late binding: every lambda reads the one shared seat variable when it runs, and by then the loop has left it set to "C3".

questions.prompt: A closure refers to a free variable from its outer function. What exactly does the closure hold onto?
choices: Nothing. It re-runs the outer function each time to recompute the variable.
Only the name of the variable, which it looks up in the global scope when called.
The variable itself, stored in a shared cell, so it sees whatever value that variable has when the closure runs.
A frozen copy of the variable's value, taken at the moment the inner function was defined.
questions.why: Python keeps each free variable in a cell shared by the outer and inner function, so the closure reads the current value at call time rather than a snapshot.

questions.prompt: A warehouse script contains: def make_tally(): total = 0; def add(n): total += n; return total; return add. A worker then runs add = make_tally() followed by add(4). What happens?
choices: It returns None, because total += n does not produce a value.
It raises UnboundLocalError, because the assignment makes total a local variable of add that is read before it has a value.
It returns 0, because total was captured as 0 when add was defined.
It returns 4, because add can read and update total from make_tally.
questions.why: Assigning to total inside add makes Python treat it as a new local, and total += n reads it first. Declaring nonlocal total would fix this.

questions.prompt: A monitoring tool builds alert checks in a loop: for t in [50, 75, 90]: checks.append(lambda x: x > t). Every check is behaving as if its threshold were 90. Which change gives each check its own threshold?
choices: Move the loop inside a function that returns checks, so t stays in an enclosing scope.
Rewrite the lambda as lambda x, t=t: x > t, so each one stores t's value as a default when it is defined.
Add nonlocal t inside each lambda, so it rebinds the loop's t.
Inspect each check's __closure__ after the loop so Python refreshes the captured values.
questions.why: Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so each lambda keeps the value t had at that moment instead of reading the shared variable later.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Python closure actually captures, using the loop-of-lambdas example. Name one limit or tradeoff of closures, such as late binding, the need for nonlocal, or memory retention.
lessons.modelAnswer: A closure is an inner function that keeps access to variables from the function that created it, even after that outer function has returned. The important detail is that it captures the variable itself, held in a shared cell, not a copy of its value. It reads the current value every time it runs. That is why three lambdas made in a loop over range(3) all return 2: they share one i, and by the time we call them the loop has left i at 2. To freeze the value, use a default argument like i=i, or a factory function that gives each closure its own cell. If the inner function needs to reassign the captured variable, declare it nonlocal, or Python treats the name as a new local. One tradeoff is memory: a closure keeps everything it captured alive, so capturing a large object holds onto that memory for as long as the function exists.
rubricPoints: A closure is an inner function that keeps access to variables from its enclosing function after that function returns.
It captures variables through shared cells, not snapshots of their values.
Late binding explains why loop-created lambdas all see the final value.
The fix is a default argument or a factory function, so each closure gets its own binding.
Reassigning a captured variable requires nonlocal, or Python raises UnboundLocalError.
A tradeoff is named, such as surprising late binding or captured objects staying alive in memory.

suggested.rationale: Predicting and then running loop-created closures, and fixing the late-binding bug, is best learned by writing and executing small Python snippets.

lessons.plain: A decorator is a way to add extra behaviour to a function without editing the function's own code. You write a small piece of logic once, such as 'record how long this took' or 'remember previous answers', and attach it to any function with a one-line label placed just above it. Think of a gift-wrapping service: the present inside stays exactly the same, but whoever receives it first meets the wrapping. The wrapping can do something before the present is reached and after it. Python itself ships several ready-made decorators for common jobs.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have twenty functions and want each one to print its own name every time it runs. Without changing the body of any of them, how might you give all twenty that behaviour by writing the printing logic only once?
lessons.teach:
A decorator is a function that takes another function and returns a replacement function. The replacement usually adds behaviour before or after calling the original, and it is called a wrapper. Placing the line @log_calls above def add(a, b) is shorthand for writing add = log_calls(add) right after the definition, so the name add now points at the wrapper.

Why it works: in Python, functions are ordinary values, so they can be passed into other functions and handed back out. The wrapper still has access to the original function because it was defined inside the decorator and can see that variable.

Worked example. Suppose log_calls defines an inner function wrapper(*args, **kwargs). The starred forms collect any positional arguments into args, which is a tuple, and any keyword arguments into kwargs, which is a dictionary, so the wrapper fits any function. Inside, wrapper prints the function's name, runs result = func(*args, **kwargs), and returns result. Then log_calls returns wrapper. Trace add(2, 3): add is now wrapper, args becomes (2, 3), it prints 'calling add', it calls the original add and gets 5, and it returns 5 to the caller.

It is good practice to put @functools.wraps(func) on the wrapper. functools is a standard library module. Its wraps decorator copies the original function's name and docstring, meaning its documentation text, onto the wrapper. Without it, error messages and debugging tools would show 'wrapper' instead of 'add'.

Several decorators are built in. @property lets a method be read like an attribute, so you write obj.area instead of obj.area(). @staticmethod marks a method that receives neither the instance nor the class. @classmethod marks a method that receives the class as its first argument, which is useful for alternative constructors. @functools.lru_cache stores each result keyed by its arguments, so a repeated call returns instantly. Storing results this way is called memoization.

Common mistake: calling func inside the wrapper but forgetting to return its result. Every decorated function then quietly returns None. In a running system nothing crashes at the decorator itself. The failure shows up later and somewhere else, for example as a report full of empty values, which makes it hard to trace.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team wants to count how often a function runs. They write a decorator called count_calls. Inside it they define an inner function wrapper(*args, **kwargs). The wrapper adds 1 to a counter, runs result = func(*args, **kwargs), and returns result. They then put @count_calls above def pack_box(items, size). That line means pack_box = count_calls(pack_box). Later a call pack_box(4, 'large') should go through the wrapper, which counts the call and hands back the original function's answer. One step is missing. After defining wrapper, what must count_calls do as its final step so the name pack_box ends up pointing at the wrapper?
choices: return wrapper(), so the wrapper runs once and its answer is stored
return wrapper, handing back the inner function itself without calling it
return func, so the original function is handed back unchanged
return result, so the counted value is handed back to pack_box
questions.why: A decorator must return the replacement function itself, so pack_box = count_calls(pack_box) leaves pack_box pointing at wrapper, which then runs on every later call.

questions.prompt: A shipping company has a decorator named audit. A developer places @audit on the line directly above def ship(order). Which plain statement does that decorator line stand for, written right after the function definition?
choices: audit(ship())
ship = audit
audit = ship(audit)
ship = audit(ship)
questions.why: The @ line is shorthand for passing the function into the decorator and rebinding the same name to whatever the decorator returns.

questions.prompt: A billing team decorates total_invoice(a, b), which normally returns a + b. Their wrapper prints a message and then runs func(*args, **kwargs), but it never returns anything. What does total_invoice(7, 8) return, and how does the problem usually show up in a running system?
choices: It returns 15, because the original function still runs inside the wrapper
It returns None, and the problem appears later, for example as empty values in a report
It returns the wrapper function itself, so a later caller gets a function object
It raises an error at the decorator line, so the program stops right away
questions.why: A wrapper that calls the original but does not return its result makes every decorated call quietly return None, so nothing crashes at the decorator and the failure surfaces somewhere else later.

questions.prompt: A delivery app has a function route_cost(city_from, city_to). It takes about 2 seconds to run, and it is called thousands of times a day with the same few city pairs. Which built-in decorator would store each result keyed by its arguments, so that a repeated call returns instantly?
choices: @functools.lru_cache
@property
@functools.wraps(func)
@staticmethod
questions.why: functools.lru_cache stores each result keyed by its arguments, so a repeat call skips the slow work. Storing results this way is called memoization.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a decorator is, what the @ line actually does, and how you would write one that works on any function. Name one built-in decorator, and describe one limit or tradeoff of using decorators.
lessons.modelAnswer: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a wrapper function that adds behaviour around it. The line @timed above def fetch() just means fetch = timed(fetch), so calling fetch actually calls the wrapper. To make a decorator work on any function, the wrapper accepts *args and **kwargs, passes them through to the original, and returns the original's result. You should also apply functools.wraps so the wrapper keeps the original name and docstring. A built-in example is functools.lru_cache, which remembers results for arguments it has seen before. The tradeoff is that the behaviour is hidden. Someone reading fetch's body won't see the caching or logging. Mistakes in the wrapper affect every decorated function. A cache like lru_cache also uses memory and can return stale data if the underlying values change.
rubricPoints: A decorator takes a function and returns a wrapper function that adds behaviour.
The @name line is shorthand for reassigning the function name to decorator(function).
The wrapper should accept *args and **kwargs and return the original function's result.
functools.wraps preserves the original function's name and docstring.
Names at least one built-in decorator such as property, staticmethod, classmethod or lru_cache.
States a tradeoff such as hidden behaviour, a silent None return, or cache memory and staleness.

suggested.rationale: Writing a decorator and watching it wrap real calls is a hands-on coding skill that no current mission exercises, so a Python drill would build it best.

lessons.plain: A unit test is a small program that checks one piece of your code, such as a single function, gives the answer you expect. pytest is a popular Python tool that finds these tests and runs them for you, then reports which passed and which failed. Think of it like a kitchen taste-tester. Each test takes one bite of a dish and says yes or no. You set up the ingredients once and reuse them, and you can taste the same recipe with many different inputs. That way, when you change the recipe later, you find out right away if something broke.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you have a function that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit and you want to check it with five different temperatures. Would you rather write five almost identical tests, or one test fed five input-and-expected-output pairs? What could go wrong with each approach?
lessons.teach:
pytest is a testing framework, meaning a tool that discovers and runs tests and reports the results. It collects files named test_*.py and runs every function in them whose name starts with test_. A test passes if it finishes without an error. It fails if an assertion is false or an exception escapes.

An assertion is a plain Python assert statement, such as assert add(2, 3) == 5. When it fails, pytest shows both sides of the comparison, so you can see what the code actually returned. To check that code raises an error, you write with pytest.raises(ValueError): and put the call inside that block. The test then passes only if that exception is raised.

A fixture is a function marked with @pytest.fixture that prepares something a test needs, such as sample data or a temporary file. A test asks for a fixture by using the fixture's name as a parameter, and pytest calls the fixture and passes in its result. Each test gets a fresh copy by default, so one test cannot pollute another.

Parametrization, written @pytest.mark.parametrize, runs one test body many times with different inputs. Each set of inputs is reported as its own separate test.

Here is a worked example. Say a function parse_port(text) should turn "80" into 80 and reject "abc". You write @pytest.mark.parametrize("text,expected", [("80", 80), ("443", 443)]) above def test_parse_port(text, expected): assert parse_port(text) == expected. pytest runs this twice, first with "80" and then with "443". A second test uses pytest.raises(ValueError) around parse_port("abc"). If parse_port wrongly returns the string "80", pytest reports that '80' does not equal 80, and that points you straight at the bug.

A common mistake is writing a test that can never fail. Examples are forgetting the assert keyword, or asserting on the same value you just computed. A test like that stays green while the code is broken. That gives false confidence, and the bug can slip into a running system unnoticed.

questions.prompt:
A bike-rental shop has a function rental_fee(hours) that should charge 6 per hour, so rental_fee(2) returns 12 and rental_fee(5) returns 30. It should raise a ValueError when hours is negative. A trainee has written most of the tests.

Step 1: @pytest.mark.parametrize("hours,expected", [(2, 12), (5, 30)]) is placed above def test_fee(hours, expected): assert rental_fee(hours) == expected. pytest runs this body twice and reports it as two separate tests.

Step 2 is missing. A second test, def test_negative_hours():, must pass only if rental_fee(-3) raises a ValueError.

Which body correctly completes Step 2?
choices: assert rental_fee(-3) == ValueError
with pytest.raises(ValueError): followed by rental_fee(-3) indented inside that block
rental_fee(-3) on its own line, with nothing else in the test
with pytest.raises(ValueError): pass, followed by rental_fee(-3) on the next line outside the block
questions.why: The test passes only when the call is placed inside the pytest.raises(ValueError) block and that exception is actually raised there.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling tests define a fixture: @pytest.fixture def open_slots(): return ["09:00", "10:00", "11:00"]. The test test_book(open_slots) removes "09:00" from the list. Later, test_count(open_slots) runs. What length does test_count see, and why?
choices: 3, because each test gets a fresh copy of the fixture's result by default
0, because a fixture can only be used by one test
It depends on the order of the tests, because fixtures share state between them
2, because test_book already removed one slot from the shared list
questions.why: pytest calls the fixture again for each test that asks for it, so test_count receives a new three-item list that test_book never touched.

questions.prompt: A weather team writes @pytest.mark.parametrize("celsius,fahrenheit", [(0, 32), (100, 212), (-40, -40), (37, 98.6)]) above one test function. How does pytest run and report this?
choices: As two tests, one for each parameter name
As four separate tests, one for each set of inputs
As one test that passes only if all four cases pass
As one test that stops after the first case passes
questions.why: Parametrization runs the same test body once per set of inputs and reports each set as its own test.

questions.prompt: A warehouse function count_boxes(orders) is broken and returns the wrong total. Which of these tests stays green even though the code is wrong?
choices: assert count_boxes(orders) == 17
total = count_boxes(orders) followed by assert total == total
assert count_boxes([]) == 0
with pytest.raises(ValueError): count_boxes(None)
questions.why: Asserting a value equals itself is always true, so the test can never fail no matter what count_boxes returns.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how assertions, fixtures and parametrization work together in pytest, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on unit tests.
lessons.modelAnswer: In pytest, each test is a function whose name starts with test_. Inside it, a plain assert states what should be true. If the assert is false, pytest shows the actual value next to the expected one. For expected errors we use pytest.raises. Fixtures are setup functions: a test lists one by name as a parameter and gets a fresh result, so shared setup isn't copied and tests don't leak state into each other. Parametrize runs one test body over many input/expected pairs, and each pair is reported as its own test, so edge cases are cheap to add. The tradeoff is that tests only check the cases we thought of. A passing suite doesn't prove the code is correct, and a badly written test that can't fail gives false confidence. Heavy fixtures can also hide what a test really depends on.
rubricPoints: Tests are test_ functions that pytest discovers, and a plain assert decides pass or fail.
pytest.raises checks that an expected exception happens.
Fixtures provide reusable, fresh setup that a test requests by parameter name.
Parametrize runs one test over many input and expected pairs, each reported separately.
Names a limit, such as tests only covering the cases you wrote, or tests that can't fail giving false confidence.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner write real tests around a config loader, so they practise assertions, expected exceptions and repeated input cases in context.

lessons.plain: Debugging means finding out why a program does something different from what you meant, then locating the exact cause. Python gives you three main tools. A traceback is the error report Python prints when a program crashes; it shows which line failed and the chain of calls that led there. A debugger is a tool that pauses a running program so you can step through it line by line and inspect values. Print debugging means adding temporary print statements to see values as the program runs. It works like a detective: read the clues first, then look closer.
lessons.guessPrompt: When Python crashes and prints a long error report listing several files and line numbers, which part do you think you should read first to understand what went wrong: the top or the bottom? Why?
lessons.teach:
A traceback is the report Python prints when an exception (an error signal raised while running) is not handled. Read it from the bottom up. The last line gives the exception type and message. Above it are frames, one per function call that was active, listed oldest first and most recent last. So the frame just above the message is where the error was raised.

Worked example. A script prints average(scores), and average returns total / len(values). The traceback shows: frame 1, report.py line 12, in <module>, calling average(scores); frame 2, report.py line 4, in average, at total / len(values); last line, ZeroDivisionError: division by zero. Trace it: the message says we divided by zero. The newest frame says that happened in average at line 4, so len(values) was 0. The older frame says line 12 passed scores in, so scores was an empty list. The real question is why scores was empty or whether average should handle that case.

A debugger lets you pause and look instead of guessing. Python's built-in one is pdb; calling breakpoint() in your code stops execution there. Common commands: n runs the next line, s steps into a function call, p shows a variable's value, c continues running.

Print debugging means adding print calls to show values. Its tradeoff: it is quick and works anywhere, even where you cannot pause the program, but each new question means editing and rerunning, and it clutters output. A debugger answers many questions in one run but takes setup and cannot easily pause a background service.

A common mistake is fixing the line where the error surfaced instead of where the bad data came from, which hides the bug. In a running system, forgotten prints flood logs and may leak private data, and a forgotten breakpoint() leaves a service frozen waiting for input that never arrives.

questions.prompt: A warehouse script crashes with this traceback. Frame 1: stock.py line 30, in <module>, calling restock(item). Frame 2: stock.py line 18, in restock, calling get_price(item). Frame 3: stock.py line 7, in get_price, at prices[name]. Last line: KeyError: 'widget'. Here is the trace, read bottom up. Step 1: the last line says a lookup used the key 'widget' and that key was not in the dictionary. Step 2: the newest frame, just above the message, says the failed lookup happened in get_price at line 7, prices[name], so name was 'widget'. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: the oldest frame says line 30 handed item to restock, so the real question is where that 'widget' value came from, or whether prices should contain it. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The frame at line 18 can be skipped, because only the newest frame and the final message ever matter in a traceback.
Frame 1 at line 30 is where the KeyError was actually raised, because the first frame listed is always the newest call.
Line 7 is the real bug, so Step 3 should wrap prices[name] in a try/except that returns 0 and lets the script keep running.
The frame at line 18 shows restock passed item into get_price, so the 'widget' value reached get_price from restock, not from inside get_price itself.
questions.why: Moving one frame older shows which caller supplied the bad value, which is how you trace the error back toward where the bad data came from instead of patching the line where it surfaced.

questions.prompt: You are paused in pdb at a line in a billing script that reads fee = compute_fee(invoice). You want to go inside compute_fee and watch it run line by line. Which pdb command do you use?
choices: n, which runs the next line
c, which continues running
p, which shows a variable's value
s, which steps into the function call
questions.why: The s command steps into the function call on the current line, while n would run the whole call and stop at the next line of the current function.

questions.prompt: A small team runs a nightly data-import job as a background service on a server. Nobody can attach a terminal to it, and it occasionally produces wrong totals. Based on the tradeoffs between print debugging and a debugger, which approach fits this situation best?
choices: Use a debugger only, because it answers many questions in one run and needs no setup.
Avoid any extra output, since prints always clutter output and are never worth using.
Add a few print calls showing key values, accepting that each new question means editing and rerunning.
Add breakpoint() inside the import loop so the job pauses and someone can inspect it when it misbehaves.
questions.why: Print debugging works even where you cannot pause the program, which suits a background service, at the cost of an edit-and-rerun cycle for each new question.

questions.prompt: A developer at a parcel-tracking company used breakpoint() to investigate a bug in their web service, fixed the bug, and deployed the code without removing the breakpoint() call. What is the most likely result once a request reaches that line?
choices: The service prints the values of every variable to the log and keeps running normally.
Python ignores breakpoint() automatically whenever the code is deployed to a server.
The service freezes at that line, waiting for debugger input that never arrives.
The service raises an exception, prints a traceback, and restarts by itself.
questions.why: breakpoint() pauses execution and waits for debugger commands, so on an unattended running service it leaves that request stuck waiting for input that nobody will type.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate's script just crashed with a long traceback and they are about to sprinkle print statements everywhere. Explain to them how to read the traceback, when a debugger is the better tool, and the tradeoffs and risks of print debugging.
lessons.modelAnswer: Start at the bottom of the traceback: the last line names the exception type and message, like ZeroDivisionError. The frame just above it is where the error was actually raised, and the frames above that show the chain of calls that got there, oldest at the top. Walk upward to find where the bad value came from, because the crash line is often just where the problem showed up, not where it started. If you still cannot tell why, use a debugger: put breakpoint() before the suspect line, then step with n or s and inspect values with p, all in one run. Prints are fine for a quick check or somewhere you cannot pause, like a background service, but every new question needs an edit and rerun. Remove them afterwards, and never leave breakpoint() in, or the service will hang waiting for input.
rubricPoints: Reads the traceback bottom-up, starting with the exception type and message.
Explains that frames run from oldest call at the top to the failing line at the bottom.
Distinguishes where the error surfaced from where the bad data originated.
Describes pausing with a debugger and inspecting or stepping through values.
Names a print-debugging tradeoff: quick and universal but needs repeated edits and reruns.
Mentions a running-system risk such as leftover prints cluttering or leaking logs, or a leftover breakpoint hanging a service.

suggested.rationale: Hardening the config loader makes the learner trigger real exceptions, read the resulting tracebacks and trace bad input back to its source before fixing it.

lessons.plain: Type hints are short labels you add to Python code saying what kind of value a variable, parameter or return value should hold, such as a whole number, a piece of text, or possibly nothing at all. Python itself ignores these labels when the program runs. A separate checking tool, called mypy, reads the code without running it and points out places where the labels disagree with how the values are used. Think of it like labelling moving boxes 'kitchen' or 'books': the boxes are not changed, but anyone checking can spot a lamp packed in the wrong box before the truck leaves.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function is labelled as sometimes returning a name and sometimes returning nothing. Some other code takes its result and immediately turns it into capital letters. Before running anything, what could go wrong, and when would you rather find out about it?
lessons.teach:
A type hint, also called an annotation, is a label attached to a name saying what type of value belongs there. You write def area(width: float, height: float) -> float: where the part after each colon labels a parameter and the part after the arrow labels the return value. A variable can be labelled too: count: int = 0.

Python does not enforce these labels at run time. They work because a static checker, a tool that analyses source code without executing it, can compare every use of a value against its label. mypy is the most common one: you run mypy on a file and it reports mismatches.

Optional[str] (from the typing module) means 'either a str or None', where None is Python's value for 'nothing here'. Newer Python also accepts str | None for the same thing. Generics are container types with their contents labelled: List[int] is a list holding ints, and Dict[str, int] is a dictionary mapping str keys to int values. Since Python 3.9 you can write the built-in forms list[int] and dict[str, int] instead.

Worked example. def find_user(user_id: int) -> Optional[str]: returns a name, or None if not found. A caller writes name = find_user(7) and then print(name.upper()). Step one: mypy sees name has type Optional[str]. Step two: it sees .upper(), which exists on str but not on None. Step three: it reports an error that upper is not an attribute of None. Adding if name is not None: before the call narrows the type to str, and the error disappears.

A common mistake is believing hints protect you at run time. Passing the string '5' to a parameter labelled int still runs, and the bug surfaces later or never. In a running system, the cost of that mistake is a crash in production, such as an error saying a None value has no attribute, which mypy would have flagged before deployment if it had been run as part of the build.

questions.prompt: A city library writes def count_loans() -> dict[str, int]: which returns a dictionary mapping each branch name to its number of current loans. Elsewhere a developer writes loans = count_loans() and then loans[42] += 1. They run mypy on the file without executing it. Step 1: mypy reads the return label and gives loans the type dict[str, int]. Step 2: ??? Step 3: mypy reports an error, and nothing has been executed. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: mypy runs the line and finds that no branch is stored under the key 42.
mypy sees the key 42 is an int, but the label says keys must be str.
Python itself rejects the int key because the annotation is enforced on use.
mypy sees the added value 1 is an int, but the label requires str values.
questions.why: In dict[str, int] the first type labels the keys, so a static checker compares the int key 42 against the str label and flags the mismatch without running anything.

questions.prompt: A weather service annotates a function as def rainfall_mm(station: str) -> Optional[float]: What does the return annotation Optional[float] tell a reader and a static checker?
choices: The function returns either a float or None, meaning 'nothing here'.
The function returns a list of floats that is allowed to be empty.
The function returns a float, but the caller may skip passing station.
mypy checks the float return value only when strict mode is on.
questions.why: Optional[X] means 'either X or None', so the function may return a float or None, and the newer spelling float | None means the same.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team needs a function tally that takes a list of product names, each a string, and returns a dictionary mapping each product name to how many times it appeared, as a whole number. Which signature labels this correctly using the built-in generic forms?
choices: def tally(names: list[int]) -> dict[int, str]:
def tally(names: dict[str, int]) -> list[str]:
def tally(names: list[str]) -> Optional[int]:
def tally(names: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]:
questions.why: list[str] labels a list holding strings, and dict[str, int] labels a dictionary with str keys and int values, which matches names in and counts out.

questions.prompt: A payments team annotates def charge(amount_cents: int) -> None: and, in another file, a developer calls charge("1500") with a string. The team deploys without ever running mypy. What happens when that line runs?
choices: Python raises an error at the call because the argument does not match the int label.
mypy runs automatically when the file is imported and stops the call.
Python automatically converts "1500" to the int 1500 because of the label.
It runs anyway, because Python does not enforce hints at run time, so the bug may surface later or never.
questions.why: Type hints are labels for static checkers only; Python ignores them when running, so without running mypy the string is passed through unchecked.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what type hints and mypy give your project, using Optional and a generic like Dict[str, int] as examples, and name one limit of relying on them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Type hints are labels on parameters, return values and variables saying what type belongs there, like width: float or a return of Optional[str], which means a string or None. Generics label what is inside a container, so Dict[str, int] says the keys are strings and the values are ints. mypy reads the code without running it and flags mismatches, for example calling .upper() on something that might be None, or putting a string value into that Dict[str, int]. That catches a whole class of mistakes before the code ships, and the labels also document intent for the next reader. The limit is that Python ignores hints at run time: if mypy is never run, or data arrives from outside such as JSON, a wrong type still gets through. So hints complement tests and input validation rather than replacing them.
rubricPoints: Defines a type hint as a label on parameters, returns or variables.
Explains Optional as 'the type or None' and why callers must check for None.
Explains a generic such as List[int] or Dict[str, int] as labelling container contents.
States that mypy checks statically, without running the code.
Names the limit that hints are not enforced at run time.

suggested.rationale: Adding annotations to a small module and fixing the mismatches mypy reports is a hands-on skill best built through repeated drills, and no current mission exercises typing.

lessons.plain: Code style is the set of habits for how code looks: how names are written, where spaces and blank lines go, how long a line can be. In Python, the shared guide is called PEP 8. A linter is a tool that reads your code without running it and points out style slips and likely mistakes, such as an import you never use or a name you never defined. Think of it like a spell checker plus a house style guide for a newspaper. Every article reads the same way, so readers focus on the story, not the formatting. Consistency matters because code is read far more often than it is written.
lessons.guessPrompt: A script imports a module at the top, never uses it, and still runs without any error. Should a tool warn about that line anyway, and what could the warning save you from?
lessons.teach:
PEP 8 is Python's official style guide. A PEP (Python Enhancement Proposal) is a design document for the language. PEP 8 recommends, among other things, four spaces per indent level, snake_case names (lowercase words joined by underscores) for functions and variables, CapWords for classes, spaces around operators, and a modest maximum line length.

A linter performs static analysis, meaning it inspects source code without executing it. flake8 is a long-standing Python linter. ruff is a newer, much faster linter that covers many of the same checks. Both report findings as rule codes. Codes starting with E or W are style issues. Codes starting with F are logical problems. A formatter, such as black or ruff's format command, goes further: it rewrites spacing and layout for you automatically.

Worked example. Consider this small module: it imports os, defines def total(items), sets x=0, loops adding each item to x, then returns y. Run the linter. Step one, it flags F401: os is imported but unused. That is clutter, and it can hide a forgotten piece of logic. Step two, it flags missing spaces around the equals sign, which is a style rule. Step three, it flags F821: undefined name y. That is a real bug. The function would crash the moment it is called, and the linter found it without running anything. You fix it by returning x.

Why consistency matters: when everyone follows one style, a code review shows only meaningful changes, newcomers can read any file, and arguments about taste disappear because the tool decides.

A common mistake is silencing warnings, either by adding a noqa comment (a marker telling the linter to skip that line) or by disabling whole rules, without first reading what each warning says. That buries genuine bugs like F821.

In a running team setup, the linter usually runs in CI (continuous integration, the automated checks that run on every change). A lint failure blocks the merge, so problems are caught before they reach production.

questions.prompt: A volunteer at a cycling club writes a small module that averages ride distances. Before opening a pull request, she runs ruff and gets three findings: line 1 F401 'sys' imported but unused; line 5 E225 missing whitespace around operator; line 9 F821 undefined name 'distnce'. She works through them. Step 1: F401 is an F code, so it is a logical problem. The unused import is clutter and might hint at forgotten logic, so she deletes it. Step 2: E225 is an E code, a style issue. She lets the formatter rewrite the spacing. Step 3: ______. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: F821 is a real bug. 'distnce' is a misspelling, so the function would crash as soon as line 9 runs. She corrects it to 'distance'.
F821 is a spacing rule like E225, so running the formatter again will clear it.
F821 is noise from a strict rule, so she adds a noqa comment to line 9 to keep CI green.
F821 only matters when the code runs, so a linter cannot be sure. She leaves it until a user reports a problem.
questions.why: An F-code undefined-name finding is a logical error the linter spots without running the code, and fixing the misspelled name removes a guaranteed crash.

questions.prompt: A linter run on a warehouse payroll script reports four rule codes: E501, W291, F811 and E302. Using only the meaning of the code prefixes, which one points to a logical problem rather than a style issue?
