questions.why: Codes starting with F report logical problems. Codes starting with E or W report style issues.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's Python module defines a class for printing labels and a function inside it. Which pair of names follows PEP 8 naming conventions?
choices: A class named shippinglabel and a function named Print_Label
A class named ShippingLabel and a function named print_label
A class named shipping_label and a function named PrintLabel
A class named Shipping_Label and a function named printLabel
questions.why: PEP 8 uses CapWords for class names and snake_case (lowercase words joined by underscores) for functions and variables.

questions.prompt: A team at a ticketing startup is tired of failed CI builds. Without reading the findings, they turn off every F rule in their linter configuration, and the lint step passes. What is the most likely consequence for their running system?
choices: Nothing changes, because F rules only cover spacing and layout that a formatter handles anyway.
Real bugs such as undefined names are no longer flagged, so they can pass the merge check and crash in production.
CI will now execute the code to find bugs instead of analysing it statically.
The code will run faster in production, because the linter no longer inspects it.
questions.why: Turning off rules without reading the warnings hides genuine logical bugs that CI would otherwise have blocked before merge.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what PEP 8 and a linter like flake8 or ruff each do, why a team should enforce one consistent style, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a linter.
lessons.modelAnswer: PEP 8 is Python's shared style guide. It covers things like four-space indents, snake_case function names, spacing around operators and line length. A linter like flake8 or ruff reads our code without running it and reports rule violations by code. Some are pure style. Others, like an unused import or an undefined name, point to real bugs we can catch before anything executes. Enforcing one style, ideally automatically in CI, keeps reviews focused on logic rather than formatting, makes every file feel familiar, and ends taste debates. The limit is that a linter only sees patterns in the text. It cannot tell whether our logic is correct, so it doesn't replace tests. There's also a tradeoff: strict rules can create noise, and the tempting shortcut of sprinkling noqa comments can hide genuine problems. Rules should be tuned deliberately, not silenced blindly.
rubricPoints: Defines PEP 8 as Python's official style guide with an example convention.
Explains that a linter statically analyses code without running it.
Notes that linters catch likely bugs such as unused imports or undefined names, not just style.
Explains that consistency makes reviews and reading easier and removes style debates.
Names a limit, such as linters not proving correctness or the danger of blanket silencing.

suggested.rationale: Running a linter on a small module, reading the rule codes and fixing both the style findings and the real bug is a hands-on drill best learned by doing.

lessons.plain: The Global Interpreter Lock, or GIL, is a rule inside the standard Python interpreter (the program that runs your Python code) that lets only one thread run Python instructions at any instant. A thread is one line of work inside a running program. Picture a kitchen with several cooks but only one knife. Cooks can wait for the oven at the same time, but only the cook holding the knife can chop. So Python threads overlap nicely while they wait on networks or disks. They do not speed up heavy calculation, because the calculating part takes turns with the single knife.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a Python program that does a big math calculation, and you split it across four threads on a four-core laptop. Do you expect it to finish about four times faster, about the same speed, or slower? What about four threads that each download a web page?
lessons.teach:
The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) is a lock inside CPython, the standard Python interpreter. A lock is a token that only one holder can have at a time. A thread must hold the GIL to run Python bytecode, which is the low-level instruction list Python compiles your code into. Only one thread holds it at a time, even on a machine with many CPU cores.

It exists because CPython tracks memory with reference counts, which are per-object tallies of how many names point at the object. Updating those tallies from several threads at once would corrupt them. One big lock is a simple, fast way to keep them safe.

What it limits: CPU-bound work, meaning work whose speed depends on the processor, such as math or image resizing. What it does not limit: I/O-bound work, meaning work that mostly waits on input/output such as network calls, disk reads or database queries. A thread releases the GIL while it waits, so another thread can run. Many C-based libraries also release it during heavy internal work. Separate processes are unaffected too. A process is an independent running program, and each one has its own interpreter and its own GIL.

Worked example. Thread A sums numbers to 50 million and Thread B does the same. A holds the GIL and runs. After a short interval it is made to hand the GIL over, then B runs, and so on. The total time is roughly the same as running them one after the other, and sometimes a bit worse because of the switching. Now suppose A and B each fetch a web page. A sends its request and releases the GIL while it waits. B sends its request during that wait. Both waits overlap, so the total time is close to a single fetch.

Common mistake: believing the GIL makes your code thread-safe. The statement count += 1 is several bytecode steps, and a thread switch can happen between them. Two threads can then lose updates. In a running system that shows up as wrong totals or double-processed jobs, so shared data still needs your own locks. Recent Python versions offer an optional build without the GIL, but the standard build still has it.

questions.prompt:
A museum's archive tool runs 4 threads in one standard CPython process. Each thread downloads one 200 MB scan from a remote storage server, and each download spends about 6 seconds just waiting for the server. Here is how the run unfolds, with one step missing.

Step 1: Thread 1 holds the GIL and runs the Python bytecode that builds and sends its download request.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: Thread 2 takes the GIL and sends its own request, and threads 3 and 4 then do the same.
Step 4: All four 6-second waits overlap, so the whole job takes close to 6 seconds instead of about 24.

Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Thread 1 starts a fresh interpreter with its own GIL, so thread 2 can use the original GIL.
Thread 1 releases the GIL while it waits for the server, so another thread can run.
The GIL splits into four copies, one per CPU core, so every thread can run bytecode at once.
Thread 1 keeps the GIL until its download finishes, so threads 2 to 4 cannot start their requests yet.
questions.why: A thread gives up the GIL while it waits on I/O, which lets the other threads send their requests during that wait so the waits overlap.

questions.prompt: In the standard build of CPython, what does the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) actually guarantee?
choices: Shared variables updated by several threads never lose an update.
Each thread is pinned to its own CPU core for the whole run.
Within one process, only one thread at a time runs Python bytecode.
Only one Python process at a time can run on the machine.
questions.why: The GIL is a single lock per interpreter that a thread must hold to run bytecode. It does not make shared data safe, and it does not restrict separate processes.

questions.prompt: A photo studio must apply a slow, pure-Python colour filter to 800 images on an 8-core machine. The work is CPU-bound, meaning its speed depends on the processor. Which approach can actually use several cores at once?
choices: Run 1 thread and make the GIL hand-over interval longer, so less time is lost to switching.
Run 8 threads in one process, because each thread gets its own core automatically.
Split the images across several processes, each with its own interpreter and its own GIL.
Run 8 threads, because a thread releases the GIL while it is doing calculations.
questions.why: Threads in one process take turns holding a single GIL for CPU-bound bytecode, but separate processes each have their own GIL, so they can run in parallel.

questions.prompt: A ticket booking service runs two threads. Each thread executes sold += 1 exactly 10,000 times on a shared variable. The final value of sold is 19,412 instead of 20,000. What is the best explanation?
choices: The += operation is several bytecode steps, and a thread switch between them lost some updates, so the code needs its own lock.
The GIL was missing because two threads cannot share one interpreter, so the counts clashed.
The threads were treated as I/O-bound, so Python skipped some increments to save time.
The GIL corrupted the reference counts of sold, which removed some of the increments.
questions.why: The GIL does not make code thread-safe. A switch can happen in the middle of the read, add and write steps of +=, so two threads can overwrite each other's updates unless you protect the shared data with your own lock.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says "Python can't do concurrency because of the GIL." Explain to them in your own words what the GIL actually limits and what it doesn't, and name one tradeoff or limit they should still watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: That's only half true. In standard CPython, the GIL is a single lock a thread must hold to run Python bytecode. That means only one thread executes Python code at a time, no matter how many cores you have. So threads won't speed up CPU-bound work like heavy number crunching, which just takes turns. But a thread releases the GIL while it waits on I/O, such as network, disk or database calls. That lets other threads run during the wait, so I/O-bound work overlaps well with threads. Separate processes each get their own GIL, and some C libraries release it during heavy computation. The tradeoff is that the GIL protects the interpreter's internals, not your data. Something like count += 1 can still be interrupted midway, so shared state needs explicit locks. Otherwise you get lost updates in production.
rubricPoints: States that the GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time in standard CPython.
Explains that CPU-bound pure-Python work gets no speedup from threads.
Explains that threads release the GIL while waiting on I/O, so I/O-bound work overlaps.
Notes that separate processes each have their own GIL.
Warns that the GIL does not make user code thread-safe, so shared data still needs locks.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is accurately explaining what the GIL does and does not restrict, and no current mission exercises Python threading directly.

lessons.plain: Some programs are slow because they wait: for a web page, a database, a disk. Others are slow because they think hard: crunching numbers, resizing images. Python offers two helpers for these cases. Threads are extra workers inside one program that share its memory; they shine when most time is spent waiting. Processes are separate copies of the program, each with its own memory, that can truly run side by side on different CPU cores; they shine when the work is heavy calculation. Picture a kitchen: one cook juggling several pots that simmer on their own (threads) versus hiring more cooks with their own stoves (processes).
lessons.guessPrompt: You need to download 10 web pages, and each one takes about 1 second, almost all of it spent waiting for the server to reply. Roughly how long would it take if 10 helpers inside the same program each fetched one page at the same time, and why?
lessons.teach:
I/O-bound work is work whose time is mostly spent waiting on input/output, such as a network reply, a file read, or a database query. CPU-bound work is work whose time is mostly spent computing on the processor. A thread is a separate line of execution inside one process, sharing that process's memory. A process is an independent running program with its own memory and its own Python interpreter.

In the standard Python interpreter (CPython), a lock called the Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python code at any instant. Threads still help with I/O because a thread that is waiting releases that lock, so other threads run while it waits. For CPU-bound work, threads take turns on one core and gain almost nothing. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and lock, so they can use several cores at once. The module concurrent.futures gives you ThreadPoolExecutor and ProcessPoolExecutor, which share the same interface, so switching is easy.

Worked example. Task A: fetch 10 URLs, each about 1 second of waiting. Sequentially: 10 seconds. With a ThreadPoolExecutor of 10 threads: all 10 requests start, all wait together, total about 1 second. Task B: compute a heavy checksum of 4 large files, each 2 seconds of pure calculation, on a 4-core machine. Sequentially: 8 seconds. With 4 threads: still about 8 seconds, because only one thread computes at a time. With a ProcessPoolExecutor of 4 processes: about 2 seconds, plus a little startup time.

Common mistake: reaching for threads for number crunching and concluding concurrency "doesn't work," or the reverse, spawning processes for many tiny tasks. Processes cost startup time and memory, and arguments and results must be copied between them (serialized), which can outweigh small jobs.

In a running system, CPU work in threads leaves one core pegged while others sit idle, and an I/O scraper built on hundreds of processes can exhaust memory. Match the tool to where the time actually goes.

questions.prompt:
A small print shop has a script that converts 6 large scanned posters into a print-ready format. Each conversion is 3 seconds of pure calculation with no waiting on files or network, and the shop's machine has 6 cores. The script runs in standard Python (CPython).

Step 1: Run sequentially. Total time is 6 x 3 = 18 seconds.
Step 2: Run with a ThreadPoolExecutor of 6 threads. Total time is ______.
Step 3: Run with a ProcessPoolExecutor of 6 processes. Each process has its own interpreter and its own lock, so all 6 conversions compute on separate cores at once. Total time is about 3 seconds, plus a little startup time.

Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: About 0.5 seconds, because threads split each 3-second conversion into six smaller pieces
About 9 seconds, because threads give roughly half the speed-up that processes give
About 3 seconds, because the 6 threads each get their own core and compute side by side
About 18 seconds, because the Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python code at a time, so the threads just take turns
questions.why: The work is CPU-bound, and in CPython the Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread compute at any instant, so the 6 threads take turns and the total stays close to the sequential 18 seconds.

questions.prompt: A weather service runs a Python program that asks 40 remote sensors for their latest reading. Each request involves about 2 seconds of waiting for the sensor to reply and almost no calculation. Which approach best fits this work?
choices: Running the requests one after another, because the Global Interpreter Lock stops any concurrency from helping
A ProcessPoolExecutor, because each request needs its own memory and its own interpreter
A ThreadPoolExecutor with a single thread, so the requests do not compete for the lock
A ThreadPoolExecutor, because a waiting thread releases the Global Interpreter Lock, so the waits overlap
questions.why: The work is I/O-bound, and threads that are waiting release the lock, so many requests can wait at the same time in one process without the extra startup time and memory that processes cost.

questions.prompt: A library's catalogue team switches a job from sequential code to a ProcessPoolExecutor. The job is 20,000 tiny tasks, each taking only a fraction of a millisecond to compute. The new version runs slower than the old one. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Starting processes and copying (serializing) every argument and result between them costs more than the tiny tasks themselves
Processes share one Global Interpreter Lock, so only one of them can compute at a time
The tasks are I/O-bound, and processes cannot wait on input/output
ProcessPoolExecutor has a different interface from ThreadPoolExecutor, so the tasks were split incorrectly
questions.why: Processes cost startup time and memory, and data must be serialized between them, and for very small jobs that overhead can outweigh any gain from using several cores.

questions.prompt: An engineering firm runs a stress-calculation service in CPython on an 8-core server. The heavy calculations are spread across 8 threads. Monitoring shows one core at 100% while the other seven sit nearly idle, and the speed is about the same as with one thread. What best explains this?
choices: Threads each run in a separate process, and the operating system is limiting them to one core
The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python code at a time, so CPU-bound threads take turns instead of using several cores
The calculations are I/O-bound, so they spend most of their time waiting rather than computing
The server needs more threads, such as 64, before all cores will be used
questions.why: For CPU-bound work in CPython, the Global Interpreter Lock forces threads to take turns, which leaves one core busy and the others idle; separate processes would be the better fit.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why you used threads for the API-polling script but processes for the image-resizing job. Explain the difference in your own words, and name one cost or limit of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: The polling script is I/O-bound: almost all its time is spent waiting for servers to answer. In CPython only one thread runs Python code at a time, but a waiting thread steps aside, so many threads can overlap their waiting and finish in roughly the time of the slowest request. Threads are cheap and share memory, though shared memory means I need care if they modify the same data. The resizing job is CPU-bound: the time goes into calculation. Threads would just take turns on one core, so I use separate processes, each with its own interpreter, to run on all cores at once. The cost is that processes take longer to start, use more memory, and must copy inputs and results between them, so for many tiny tasks that overhead can erase the gain.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes I/O-bound (waiting) from CPU-bound (computing) work.
Explains that threads help I/O because waiting threads let others run, but only one thread runs Python code at a time.
Explains that processes have separate interpreters and memory, so they can use multiple cores for CPU work.
Names a cost of processes such as startup time, memory use, or copying data between them.
Names a limit of threads such as no CPU speedup or the need to protect shared data.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is diagnosing whether a stated workload is waiting or computing and justifying the tool, which is best practiced by reasoning through short exam-style scenarios.

lessons.plain: Asynchronous programming lets one program juggle many waiting tasks without sitting idle. Think of a cook making breakfast: put toast in, and while it browns, crack eggs, then pour coffee while the eggs fry. One cook, one pair of hands, but nothing waits on anything else. In Python, the asyncio library is the kitchen manager. You mark functions that may need to wait (for a network reply, a file, a timer) with async, and at each waiting point you say await, which means "I'm paused, go do something else and come back when my thing is ready." It shines when most of the time is spent waiting, not computing.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need to fetch three web pages, and each one takes about 1 second to reply. If one worker sends all three requests and then waits for whichever reply comes back first, roughly how long does the whole job take: about 1 second or about 3 seconds? Why?
lessons.teach:
Asynchronous programming means writing code that can pause at waiting points so other work runs meanwhile, all on a single thread. A thread is one line of execution inside a program. Python's standard library module asyncio provides the event loop, which is a scheduler that keeps a list of paused tasks and resumes each one when the thing it was waiting for is ready.

Three terms matter. A coroutine is a function defined with async def. Calling it does not run its body; it returns a coroutine object that the event loop can run. The keyword await, used only inside a coroutine, says: pause me here until this other awaitable finishes, and let the loop run something else. An awaitable is anything you can await, such as another coroutine or a task. A task wraps a coroutine so the loop runs it concurrently. asyncio.run(main()) starts the loop and runs a top coroutine, and asyncio.gather(a, b, c) runs several awaitables concurrently and returns all their results.

Why it works: during network or disk waits the CPU is idle, so switching to another task costs almost nothing. This only helps I/O-bound work, which is work dominated by waiting.

Worked example: three coroutines each do await asyncio.sleep(1), standing in for a 1-second network call. With gather, the loop starts the first, which hits await and pauses. The loop starts the second, which pauses, then the third, which pauses. About 1 second later all three timers are done and each resumes in turn. Total is about 1 second, not 3.

Common mistake: calling a blocking function inside a coroutine, such as time.sleep(1) or a synchronous HTTP library. Blocking code never yields control, so the whole event loop freezes and every other task stalls. In a running service this shows up as every request slowing down at once. A related mistake is forgetting await, which leaves a coroutine that never runs. CPU-heavy loops also block the loop, so asyncio is the wrong tool for number crunching.

questions.prompt: A cycling club's weather dashboard gets forecasts from 4 regional servers. Each request is a coroutine that awaits a network reply, and each reply takes about 2 seconds. main() passes all four to asyncio.gather and is started with asyncio.run(main()). Here is the trace with one step missing. Step 1: the event loop starts the coroutine for region A. It reaches its await and pauses. Step 2: ???. Step 3: about 2 seconds later all four replies have arrived, and each coroutine resumes in turn and returns its forecast. Step 4: gather hands back all four forecasts, and the total time is about 2 seconds, not 8. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The loop creates a separate thread for each of regions B, C and D so that they can wait in parallel.
The loop resumes A straight away and sends its request again and again until the reply arrives.
The loop waits the full 2 seconds for region A to finish before it starts region B, because there is only one thread.
While A is paused, the loop starts B, then C, then D. Each one reaches its await and pauses too.
questions.why: Each await hands control back to the single-threaded loop, so it starts the next task. All four waits then overlap, which is why the total is about 2 seconds.

questions.prompt: A developer at a ticketing startup defines async def fetch_seats(). Inside another coroutine they write fetch_seats() on its own line, with no await and no gather. What happens to the body of fetch_seats?
choices: It runs right away and finishes, just like a normal function call.
The event loop automatically picks it up and runs it in the background.
Python refuses to start the program and reports a syntax error.
It never runs. The call only creates a coroutine object, and nothing hands that object to the event loop.
questions.why: Calling a coroutine function only returns a coroutine object. Without await, or wrapping it so the loop runs it, the body never runs.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing service handles uploads with asyncio. To slow down heavy users, a developer adds time.sleep(3) inside the async upload handler. When traffic rises, what will the operators most likely see?
choices: Python quietly treats time.sleep as asyncio.sleep inside a coroutine, so nothing changes.
Every request across the service slows down at once, because the blocking sleep freezes the whole event loop.
The event loop opens a new thread for each sleeping handler, so the other requests carry on normally.
Only the heavy user's upload takes 3 seconds longer, and everyone else is unaffected.
questions.why: time.sleep is a blocking call that never hands control back to the loop. While it sleeps, every other task on that single thread is stalled.

questions.prompt: Which of these jobs is the best fit for asyncio?
choices: A crawler that downloads 500 pages from different websites and spends most of its time waiting on the network
Calculating every prime number below 50 million with a pure Python loop
Resizing thousands of images by changing pixels one at a time in Python code
Running a heavy statistics calculation over a large table that is already held in memory
questions.why: asyncio helps only with I/O-bound work, meaning work dominated by waiting. The other three jobs are CPU-heavy, and CPU-heavy loops block the event loop.

lessons.explainPrompt: In your own words, explain to a teammate how async/await and the asyncio event loop let one thread handle many network calls, and name one situation where asyncio would not help or would cause problems.
lessons.modelAnswer: With asyncio, a single thread runs an event loop that schedules coroutines, which are functions written with async def. When a coroutine reaches an await on something slow, like a network reply, it pauses and hands control back to the loop, which resumes another coroutine that is ready. Because I/O waits leave the CPU idle, overlapping them is nearly free: three 1-second calls run with asyncio.gather finish in about 1 second instead of 3. The catch is that it is cooperative. Switching only happens at await points, so if any code blocks, such as time.sleep or a synchronous HTTP library, the entire loop freezes and every task stalls. It also doesn't help CPU-bound work, like heavy calculations, because there is no waiting to overlap; the computation just hogs the single thread. Every library in the call path also needs to be async-aware.
rubricPoints: States that async def defines a coroutine and await marks a point where it pauses and yields control.
Explains that a single-threaded event loop schedules and resumes paused tasks.
Explains the benefit comes from overlapping I/O waits, for example with gather.
Names that blocking calls inside a coroutine freeze the whole loop.
Notes asyncio does not speed up CPU-bound work.

suggested.rationale: Writing and timing small coroutines, and seeing a blocking call stall the loop, is best learned by running code in a Python drill environment, which no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: Profiling means measuring where a program actually spends its time before you try to make it faster. Programmers are often wrong when they guess which part is slow, so they measure first. Python includes two built-in measuring tools. timeit is a stopwatch for one small piece of code: it runs the piece many times and reports how long it took. cProfile is more like an itemised receipt for a whole program: it lists every function that ran, how many times it ran, and how much time it used. Think of a mechanic who checks the engine with a diagnostic tool instead of replacing random parts and hoping the car runs better.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your report script takes 10 seconds. One function in it takes 9 of those seconds and another takes 0.2 seconds. If you made the 0.2-second function twice as fast, roughly how long would the script take to run now?
lessons.teach:
Profiling is measuring where a program spends its time. Optimizing is changing code to make it faster. The rule is to profile before you optimize, because effort spent on code that is not slow cannot speed up the program much.

The bottleneck is the part of the program that uses most of the time. timeit is a standard-library module that runs a small snippet many times and reports the total time. Repeating the snippet smooths out random noise from the computer, so timeit suits head-to-head comparisons, such as two ways to build a list. cProfile is a standard-library profiler. It records every function call and prints a table. In that table, ncalls is how many times a function ran. tottime is the time spent inside the function's own code. cumtime, or cumulative time, is that time plus the time spent in every function it called.

Worked example: a log report takes 10 seconds. First, run the script under cProfile and sort the table by cumtime. Second, read the table. It shows that parse_line ran 200,000 times, and inside it a function called is_known_host uses 8.5 seconds of tottime. Third, look at is_known_host and find that it searches a list of hosts for every line. Fourth, write a version that stores the hosts in a set, which can check membership quickly. Fifth, use timeit to compare the two versions: the list version takes 40 microseconds per call and the set version takes 0.05 microseconds. Finally, re-run cProfile. The script now finishes in about 1.5 seconds.

A common mistake is to rewrite code that "looks slow" without measuring it. If that code used only 2% of the runtime, even a perfect rewrite saves almost nothing. Meanwhile the change can add bugs and make the code harder to read. Note also that profilers add overhead, meaning extra cost from the measuring itself. Treat the times as relative, not exact.

In a running system, profiling tells you whether a slowdown comes from computation or from waiting on disk or network. That answer decides which kind of fix is worth trying.

questions.prompt: A bakery's order-export script takes 30 seconds to run. Step 1: the developer runs the script under cProfile, a standard-library profiler that records every function call, and sorts the table by cumtime (a function's own time plus the time of every function it calls). Step 2: the table shows export_orders with a cumtime of 29 seconds. Inside it, format_price ran 50,000 times with 0.6 seconds of tottime (time spent in its own code), and lookup_customer ran 50,000 times with 24 seconds of tottime. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the developer writes a new lookup_customer that keeps customers in a dictionary keyed by customer ID. Step 5: timeit compares the old and new lookup_customer. Step 6: cProfile is run again to confirm the whole script got faster. Which choice best fills Step 3?
choices: Rewrite format_price first, because price formatting with string operations usually looks slow and is called 50,000 times.
Open lookup_customer, because it has by far the largest tottime, and find that it searches a full list of customers on every call.
Stop using cProfile, because its overhead means the 24-second figure cannot be trusted at all.
Rewrite export_orders itself, because it has the largest cumtime of any function in the table.
questions.why: lookup_customer spends 24 of the 30 seconds in its own code, so it is the bottleneck, and inspecting it is what leads to the dictionary fix in Step 4.

questions.prompt: In a cProfile table, a function called build_report shows a tottime of 0.2 seconds and a cumtime of 6.0 seconds. What does this tell you?
choices: Most of the 6 seconds is spent in functions that build_report calls, not in its own code.
build_report's own code is the bottleneck and should be rewritten first.
The profiler's overhead added 5.8 seconds, so the real time is 0.2 seconds.
build_report ran 6 times, and each run took 0.2 seconds.
questions.why: cumtime includes time in called functions while tottime is only the function's own code, so the 5.8-second gap belongs to the functions it calls.

questions.prompt: A developer wants to know which of two small ways to combine 1,000 strings into one is faster, and wants a fair head-to-head result that is not thrown off by random noise from the computer. Which tool fits best?
choices: Running each version once and comparing a single wall-clock reading.
timeit, which runs each small snippet many times and reports the total time.
cProfile on the whole application, reading the ncalls column.
Rewriting both versions to look simpler and choosing the shorter one.
questions.why: timeit repeats a small snippet many times to smooth out noise, which makes it suited to comparing two ways of doing the same small task.

questions.prompt: A data job takes 20 seconds. Without profiling, a developer spends a day rewriting a function that looked slow. A later cProfile run shows that function used only 3% of the runtime. Even if the rewrite made that function take zero time, about how much faster could the job get?
choices: About 3 seconds, so the job would take roughly 17 seconds.
About 17 seconds, because a perfect rewrite removes most of the cost.
About 0.6 seconds, so the job would still take roughly 19.4 seconds.
About 10 seconds, because rewriting any function roughly halves runtime.
questions.why: 3% of 20 seconds is 0.6 seconds, so even a perfect rewrite of code that is not the bottleneck saves almost nothing, while still risking new bugs.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to speed up a slow script by rewriting a loop they suspect is inefficient. Explain to them, in your own words, why and how to profile first using cProfile and timeit, and name one limit of these measurements.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before rewriting anything, we should measure, because people often guess wrong about what is slow. I'd run the whole script under cProfile and sort the results by cumulative time, which is the time spent in a function plus everything it calls. That shows the bottleneck, the function eating most of the runtime, along with how many times it was called. If your loop only accounts for 3% of the time, a rewrite saves at most 3%. Once we know the real hotspot, we can write an alternative and use timeit to compare the old and new versions. timeit runs each version many times, so random noise averages out. Then we re-profile to confirm the overall gain. One limit is that profiling adds its own overhead, so the numbers are relative rather than exact. Another is that results depend on the input we test with, so we should use realistic data.
rubricPoints: States that you measure before optimizing because guesses about slow code are often wrong.
Explains that cProfile shows per-function call counts and time across a whole program, revealing the bottleneck.
Explains that timeit repeatedly times a small snippet to compare alternatives reliably.
Notes that speeding up a part that uses little of the total time gives little overall gain.
Names a limit such as profiler overhead, relative rather than exact timings, or dependence on realistic input.

suggested.rationale: Profiling only sticks once you have run cProfile on slow code, read the table, and confirmed a fix with timeit, and a Python drills engine would let the learner do exactly that.

lessons.plain: Many websites and services offer an API (application programming interface): a set of web addresses your program can ask for data instead of a person clicking around. Your program sends a request over HTTP, the same protocol browsers use, and gets back a response, usually written in JSON, a plain-text format of nested lists and key-value pairs. The requests library is a popular Python add-on that makes sending those requests short and readable. Think of it like ordering at a counter: you ask clearly, wait a sensible time, check you got what you ordered, then unpack the bag.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your program asks a web service for a user's details and the service replies 'not found', should your program carry on as if it got the data, or check first? What could go wrong if it carries on?
lessons.teach:
An HTTP API is a service that answers requests sent to URLs (web addresses). A GET request asks to read data. Every response carries a status code: a number where 200 means success, 404 means not found, and 500-range means the server failed. The body is often JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), text that maps neatly onto Python dictionaries and lists.

The requests library, installed separately with pip, wraps this up. requests.get(url, params=..., timeout=5) sends a GET; params adds query values to the URL for you; timeout is how many seconds to wait before giving up. It returns a Response object. response.status_code holds the number, response.raise_for_status() raises an HTTPError exception if the code is 400 or above, and response.json() parses the body into Python objects.

Worked example: you want the name of user 3. Step 1: call requests.get('https://api.example.com/users', params={'id': 3}, timeout=5). requests builds the URL ending in ?id=3 and sends it. Step 2: the server replies with status 200 and body {"id": 3, "name": "Ana"}. Step 3: raise_for_status() sees 200 and does nothing. Step 4: data = response.json() gives the dictionary {'id': 3, 'name': 'Ana'}. Step 5: data.get('name') returns 'Ana'. Had the server replied 404, step 3 would raise, and your except block would log it instead of crashing later with a confusing KeyError.

A common mistake is leaving out timeout. By default requests waits indefinitely, so one slow or dead server can freeze your script forever. A second mistake is calling .json() without checking the status; an error page may not be JSON at all, giving a decoding error far from the real cause.

In a running system, wrap calls in try/except for requests.exceptions.RequestException (the parent of connection, timeout and HTTP errors), always set a timeout, and treat missing JSON keys as possible. Because the program spends most of its time waiting on the network, this is I/O-bound work.

questions.prompt: A bookshop's script checks stock for one book. Step 1: it calls requests.get('https://api.bookshop.test/stock', params={'isbn': '9780141439518'}, timeout=8), and requests adds ?isbn=9780141439518 to the URL. Step 2: the stock server is having trouble and replies with status code 503 and an HTML error page. Step 3: the script calls response.raise_for_status() inside a try block that has an except clause for requests.exceptions.RequestException. Step 4 is missing. What happens at step 4?
choices: requests notices the 503 and automatically repeats the request until the server replies with 200.
Nothing happens at step 3, because raise_for_status() only raises for 404, so the script later fails with a KeyError.
raise_for_status() raises an HTTPError because 503 is 400 or above, the except block catches it and logs it, and response.json() is never reached.
raise_for_status() returns False, so the script continues and response.json() parses the HTML page into a dictionary.
questions.why: raise_for_status() raises HTTPError for any status code of 400 or above, and HTTPError is a kind of RequestException, so the except block handles it before the script tries to parse a body that is not JSON.

questions.prompt: A transit company's script asks a train-times API for departures every minute using requests.get('https://api.trains.test/departures'). One night the API server stops responding without closing the connection, and the script freezes and never prints anything again. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The URL had no params argument, so requests could not finish building the request.
The status code was 500, and requests keeps waiting until a server sends a 200.
The response body was not JSON, so response.json() looped forever.
No timeout was given, and by default requests waits indefinitely for a reply.
questions.why: Without a timeout argument, requests waits forever, so a single dead or very slow server can freeze the whole script.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointment script calls a scheduling API. You want one except clause that handles a failed connection, a request that took longer than its timeout, and an error status raised by raise_for_status(). Which exception should you catch?
choices: ValueError
requests.exceptions.RequestException
requests.exceptions.HTTPError
KeyError
questions.why: RequestException is the parent of connection errors, timeout errors and HTTP errors, so catching it covers all three cases.

questions.prompt: A developer at a weather startup writes data = requests.get('https://api.weather.test/today', params={'city': 'Lyon'}, timeout=6).json(), calling .json() immediately without checking the status. The server replies with status 502 and an HTML error page. What is the most likely result?
choices: response.json() returns an empty dictionary, and the script carries on safely.
The params argument is dropped, and the request is sent again without ?city=Lyon.
requests changes the status code to 200, because the timeout was set.
A decoding error is raised, because the error page is not JSON, and it hides the real cause, which was the 502 status.
questions.why: An error page may not be JSON at all, so calling .json() without checking the status gives a decoding error that points away from the real problem, the failed request.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would fetch data from an HTTP API with requests and turn the reply into Python data safely. Name at least one limit or tradeoff, such as what happens without a timeout or when the server returns an error.
lessons.modelAnswer: I call requests.get with the URL, any query values in params, and always a timeout, say five seconds. That returns a Response. I call raise_for_status so any 4xx or 5xx status becomes an exception right away, then response.json() to turn the JSON body into dictionaries and lists, and I read fields with .get so a missing key doesn't crash me. I wrap it all in try/except for RequestException, which covers connection failures, timeouts and bad statuses. The tradeoff with timeout: too short and you fail on a merely slow server, but no timeout means one dead server can hang the whole script forever. Also, if I skip the status check, an error page might not be JSON, so I'd get a confusing decode error instead of the real problem. Each call mostly waits on the network, so it's I/O-bound.
rubricPoints: Uses requests.get with a URL and optional params to send the request.
Always sets a timeout and explains the risk of hanging without one.
Checks the status code, for example with raise_for_status, before trusting the body.
Parses the body with response.json() into dictionaries and lists and reads keys defensively.
Catches request exceptions so network failures are handled, not crashed on.
Recognises that API calls are I/O-bound because time is spent waiting on the network.

suggested.rationale: Writing and running small request-and-parse drills, including error and timeout cases, builds the habit better than reading, and no current mission has the learner call an HTTP API from Python.

lessons.plain: An end-to-end project is one small program that goes all the way from raw input to a finished, useful output, using many skills at once instead of one at a time. Earlier units taught pieces separately: loops, functions, classes, files, error handling, tests, type hints, and concurrency (doing several tasks at overlapping times). Here you snap those pieces together. Think of building a bookshelf after practising sawing, drilling and sanding on scrap wood. Each skill was fine alone, but the real lesson is how the parts fit, in what order, and where they tend to wobble.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need a script that reads 50 website addresses from a file, checks whether each one responds, and writes a summary report. Before writing any code, what separate pieces would you split the job into, and which piece do you think will be slowest?
lessons.teach:
Integrating units means designing one program as a pipeline: a chain of small stages where each stage takes data in and hands data on. Each stage is a function, a named reusable block of code. Keeping stages separate lets you test each one alone.

A typical shape has four stages: load (read input such as a CSV file, a text file of comma-separated rows), model (turn rows into structured objects, for example a dataclass, a class that mainly holds named fields), process (do the real work), and report (write output such as JSON, a text format for structured data). An entry point, a main() function, calls the stages in order. Type hints, labels showing what type each function expects and returns, document the hand-offs. Unit tests, small automatic checks of one function, guard each stage. Error handling with try/except stops one bad row from crashing the whole run.

Worked example: a website checker. Step 1, load reads sites.csv with three rows: example.org, bad url, example.net. Step 2, model turns valid rows into Site(name, url) objects. The bad row raises an error that is caught, logged and skipped, so two Sites remain. Step 3, process checks each site and records a status and a response time. Waiting on a network reply is I/O-bound work, meaning time is spent waiting rather than computing, so a small thread pool can overlap the waits. Step 4, report counts two checked, one skipped, and writes summary.json.

A common mistake is writing everything as one long script, then adding concurrency before the plain version even works. The bug becomes very hard to locate, and you cannot tell whether the speed-up was needed. Build the simple sequential version first, test it, measure it, then add concurrency only to the stage that is actually slow. In a running system, a pipeline with clear stages fails in one known place and keeps the rest of its output, while a tangled script tends to fail all at once.

questions.prompt: A bakery builds a small order summarizer as a pipeline. Step 1, load: it reads orders.csv, which has 6 rows. Step 2, model: it turns each row into an Order(customer, item, qty) dataclass object. Row 4 has the quantity written as "lots", which raises an error when converting it to a number. Step 3: ??? Step 4, process: it adds up the quantity for each item across the 5 valid Order objects. Step 5, report: it writes totals.json saying 5 orders processed and 1 skipped. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The error stops the program with a traceback, and totals.json is never written.
Row 4 is quietly given a quantity of 0 and counted as a processed order.
The whole file is rejected because one row is bad, and the user is asked to fix it before anything runs.
The error is caught with try/except, logged and skipped, so the 5 valid Orders continue to the process stage.
questions.why: The report shows 5 processed and 1 skipped, which only happens if the bad row's error is caught, logged and skipped while the valid rows carry on.

questions.prompt: A developer designs a program as a pipeline, a chain of stages that each take data in and hand data on. What is the main benefit of writing each stage as its own separate function?
choices: It allows the whole program to be written as one long script without an entry point.
It makes the program run faster, because separate functions run at the same time automatically.
It removes the need for type hints, because each function name already explains its job.
Each stage can be tested on its own with a unit test, so a problem can be traced to one stage.
questions.why: Keeping stages separate lets you guard and test each one alone, so failures show up in one known place.

questions.prompt: A city parking office has a tool that asks 30 garage sensors over the network for their current occupancy, then writes a report. The plain sequential version works and its unit tests pass. Timing shows that about 95% of the run is spent in the fetch stage, waiting for sensor replies. What is the best next step?
choices: Merge all the stages into one long script so there are fewer function calls to slow it down.
Add concurrency to every stage, including load and report, so the whole program is concurrent.
Add a small thread pool to the fetch stage only, so the network waits overlap.
Leave it as it is, because waiting on a network is CPU-bound work that concurrency cannot help.
questions.why: Waiting on network replies is I/O-bound work, and after measuring, concurrency should be added only to the stage that is actually slow.

questions.prompt: A student writes a file-renaming tool as one long script and adds threads straight away, before a plain version has ever worked. The tool now sometimes produces wrong results. According to good pipeline practice, what is the most likely consequence of this approach?
choices: The bug will be confined to one known stage, and the rest of the output will be kept.
The bug is very hard to locate, and the student cannot tell whether the speed-up was even needed.
The type hints will automatically point to the line that caused the wrong results.
Nothing serious, because adding threads early always makes bugs easier to spot.
questions.why: Adding concurrency to a tangled script before a tested, measured sequential version exists hides where the bug is and whether concurrency was needed at all.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would structure a small end-to-end Python project from input file to report, and name one tradeoff, such as when adding concurrency is worth its extra complexity.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd build it as a pipeline of small functions: load the input, turn rows into a dataclass, process each item, then write a JSON report, with a main() that calls them in order. Type hints show what each stage hands to the next, and I'd write a unit test per stage so I can trust each piece separately. Bad input gets caught with try/except and logged, so one broken row doesn't kill the run. I'd get a plain sequential version working first. Only if measuring shows one stage is slow would I add concurrency, for example threads for network checks, since that work is mostly waiting. The tradeoff is that concurrency adds complexity and harder debugging, so it's only worth it when the speed gain is real and the work suits it.
rubricPoints: Splits the project into clear stages such as load, model, process and report.
Uses functions, a data structure like a dataclass, and a main entry point to connect stages.
Mentions tests and type hints to make hand-offs between stages reliable.
Handles bad input without crashing the whole run.
Builds a working simple version before adding concurrency or optimizing.
Names a tradeoff, such as concurrency adding complexity that is only justified for slow, waiting-heavy work.

suggested.rationale: The CSV-to-JSON fleet report already makes the learner chain loading, modelling, processing and reporting into one working end-to-end program.

scenarios.title: Tracing the Bin Stock Checker at Brightwell Bakery Supplies
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined the warehouse tools team at Brightwell Bakery Supplies, a fictional company that stores flour, sugar and packaging in numbered storage bins. A colleague left behind a short Python script that checks five bins and reports which ones are running low. Before anyone changes it, your lead asks you to trace it by hand. Tracing means reading the code one line at a time and keeping track of every variable's value, just as the computer would.

Here is the script exactly as written. Indentation, the spaces at the start of a line, shows which lines belong inside a loop or an if block.

threshold = 5
low_count = 0
for bin_no in range(1, 6):
    qty = bin_no * 4 % 10
    if qty == 0:
        print(f"Bin {bin_no}: EMPTY")
        continue
    elif qty < threshold:
        print(f"Bin {bin_no}: low ({qty})")
        low_count += 1
    else:
        print(f"Bin {bin_no}: ok")
    if qty > 7:
        print(f"Overstock in bin {bin_no}, stopping scan")
        break
else:
    print("Scan complete")
if low_count:
    print(f"Reorder needed for {low_count} bin(s)")
else:
    print("No reorder needed")

Some reminders. range(1, 6) produces the whole numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order. It stops just before the second number. The % operator, called modulo, gives the remainder after division, so 12 % 10 is 2. The * and % operators have equal precedence, meaning equal priority, so Python works through them from left to right. The line bin_no * 4 % 10 therefore multiplies first and then takes the remainder.

An f-string is a string written with an f before the opening quote. Python replaces anything inside curly braces with that variable's current value.

The word continue skips the rest of the current loop pass and moves to the next value. The word break leaves the loop entirely. The else attached to a for loop, called the loop else clause, runs only if the loop finished all its passes without hitting break.

Truthiness is the rule that lets Python treat a non-boolean value as True or False in a condition. The number 0 counts as False, and any other number counts as True.

1. Trace the script as written and give its exact printed output, line by line.
2. Your lead changes only the line if qty > 7: to if qty > 9: and leaves everything else the same. Give the new exact printed output and explain why "Scan complete" does or does not appear.
3. A teammate wants staff to type the threshold, so they replace threshold = 5 with threshold = input("Threshold: "). When someone types 5, the script crashes with a TypeError, which is the error Python raises when an operation is used on a type it does not support. Explain why it crashes and give the one-line fix.
subParts: Predict the original output
Predict output after the limit change
Explain and fix the input() crash
modelAnswer:
The output is exactly four lines:

Bin 1: low (4)
Bin 2: ok
Overstock in bin 2, stopping scan
Reorder needed for 1 bin(s)

Pass for bin_no = 1: qty = 1 * 4 % 10, which is 4 % 10, which is 4. Is 4 == 0? No. Is 4 < 5? Yes, so it prints "Bin 1: low (4)" and low_count becomes 1. Then it checks 4 > 7, which is False, so there is no break.

Pass for bin_no = 2: qty = 2 * 4 % 10, which is 8 % 10, which is 8. Is 8 == 0? No. Is 8 < 5? No. So the else branch prints "Bin 2: ok". Then 8 > 7 is True, so it prints "Overstock in bin 2, stopping scan" and break exits the loop. Bins 3 to 5 are never checked.

Because the loop ended with break, the loop else is skipped, so "Scan complete" is not printed. Finally, low_count is 1. A non-zero number is truthy, so it prints "Reorder needed for 1 bin(s)".

The output is exactly seven lines:

Bin 1: low (4)
Bin 2: ok
Bin 3: low (2)
Bin 4: ok
Bin 5: EMPTY
Scan complete
Reorder needed for 2 bin(s)

Trace: bin 1 has qty 4, which is low, so low_count becomes 1. 4 > 9 is False.
Bin 2 has qty 8, which is ok. 8 > 9 is False.
Bin 3 has qty 12 % 10, which is 2. That is low, so low_count becomes 2. 2 > 9 is False.
Bin 4 has qty 16 % 10, which is 6. That is ok. 6 > 9 is False.
Bin 5 has qty 20 % 10, which is 0. The script prints "Bin 5: EMPTY" and continue skips the overstock check for that pass.

No value is ever greater than 9, so break never runs. The loop uses up all five values from range and ends normally, so the loop else runs and prints "Scan complete". Note that continue does not stop the else clause from running; only break does. low_count is 2, which is truthy, so the last line is "Reorder needed for 2 bin(s)".

input() always returns a str, which is text, even when the person types digits. So threshold becomes the string "5", not the int 5. On the first pass, the script reaches qty < threshold, which compares the int 4 with the str "5". Python does not allow < between a number and text, so it raises a TypeError and the program stops. In a running tool, that means the scan stops before any bins are reported.

The fix is to convert the text to a whole number: threshold = int(input("Threshold: ")). With that change, typing 5 makes threshold the int 5, and the script behaves exactly as in the original trace.

scenarios.title: The parcel labels that kept multiplying at Fernbrook Freight
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Fernbrook Freight, a fictional parcel-delivery company, as a junior engineer. A teammate wrote some small Python helpers for the warehouse scanning tool and asks you to review them before they go live.

A few terms first. A function is a named block of code you can run again and again by calling it. A parameter is a name in the function's definition that receives a value when the function is called. A default argument is a value written into the definition, such as labels=[], that Python uses when the caller leaves that parameter out. A keyword argument is a value passed by naming the parameter in the call, such as labels=['fragile'], instead of relying on position. A list is an ordered collection, written with square brackets. It is mutable, meaning it can be changed in place after it is created.

Helper A:

def add_label(parcel_id, labels=[]):
    labels.append('checked')
    return {'id': parcel_id, 'labels': labels}

a = add_label('P1')
b = add_label('P2')
print(b['labels'])

Helper B:

def report_total(weights):
    total = sum(weights)
    print('Total:', total)

result = report_total([2, 3])

A return value is what a function hands back to its caller through a return statement. A side effect is anything a function does that is visible outside it apart from that returned value, such as printing to the screen.

Helper C:

threshold = 10
def is_heavy(weight):
    threshold = 20
    return weight > threshold

print(is_heavy(15), threshold)

Scope is the region of code where a name can be seen and used. The LEGB rule is the order in which Python searches for a name: Local (inside the current function), Enclosing (inside any outer function that wraps this one), Global (the top level of the file), then Built-in (names Python always provides, like print or sum).

A docstring is a string written as the first line inside a function's body. It describes what the function does, and tools such as help() can read it.

Your tasks:
1. For Helper A, predict exactly what print(b['labels']) shows. Explain why, using the idea of a default value and a mutable list.
2. Rewrite add_label so that each call without a labels argument gets a fresh list. Add a one-line docstring, and show one example call that passes labels as a keyword argument.
3. For Helper B, state the value of result and explain why. Say what a caller hoping to use the total will run into.
4. For Helper C, predict the printed output and explain it using the LEGB rule.
subParts: Predict the mutable-default output
Fix add_label with docstring and keyword call
Return value vs. side effect in report_total
Predict scope behavior with LEGB
modelAnswer:
It prints ['checked', 'checked'].

Python creates a default value once, when the def line runs, not each time the function is called. So every call that leaves out labels shares that same single list. The first call, add_label('P1'), appends 'checked', and the shared list becomes ['checked']. The second call, add_label('P2'), appends to that same list again, giving ['checked', 'checked'].

Because a['labels'] and b['labels'] are the same list object, a now also shows two labels. In the running scanning tool, every parcel processed without explicit labels would pile up the labels of all earlier parcels, and the list would keep growing for as long as the program runs.

result is None.

report_total prints 'Total: 5' as a side effect, but it has no return statement. A Python function that ends without return automatically returns None.

A caller who writes something like result + 1 to use the total will get an error, because None cannot be added to a number. Code that saves result will store None instead of 5. The fix is to add return total, and to print only if printing is actually wanted.

It prints False 10.

The assignment threshold = 20 inside is_heavy creates a new local variable that exists only inside that function. When the function evaluates weight > threshold, Python looks up threshold using LEGB and finds the Local one first, which is 20. The check 15 > 20 is False.

The global threshold is never touched, so the print outside the function finds the Global threshold, which is still 10. A common mistake is to assume that the assignment inside the function changes the global. It does not, unless the function declares global threshold.

scenarios.title: Brightleaf Logistics: Sorting Out the Morning Order Log
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightleaf Logistics, a fictional small warehouse company, as a junior developer. Each morning a script reads the order log into Python as a list of dicts. A list is an ordered, changeable sequence of items written in square brackets, where position 0 is the first item. A dict (dictionary) is a lookup table that maps each unique key to a value, written in curly braces as key: value pairs. A tuple is an ordered sequence like a list but immutable, meaning it cannot be changed after it is created. It is written in round brackets. A set is an unordered collection that keeps only one copy of each item and can check membership very quickly.

Here is the data your teammate Priya loaded:

orders = [{'id': 'A1', 'customer': 'Rosa', 'day': 'Mon', 'bin': (3, 7)}, {'id': 'A2', 'customer': 'Theo', 'day': 'Mon', 'bin': (1, 2)}, {'id': 'A3', 'customer': 'Rosa', 'day': 'Tue', 'bin': (3, 7)}, {'id': 'A4', 'customer': 'Kemi', 'day': 'Tue', 'bin': (5, 0)}]

Each 'bin' value is a storage location given as (aisle, shelf). Dict keys must be hashable. A hashable value is one Python can turn into a fixed fingerprint so it can find the key again later. In practice that means the value must be unchangeable, so tuples of numbers are hashable and lists are not.

Priya wants several quick views of this data. Where she asks for a comprehension, write one. A comprehension is a one-line expression that loops over items and builds a new list, dict or set from them, for example {x: x * 2 for x in nums}.

1. Priya asks why bin locations are stored as tuples like (3, 7) instead of lists like [3, 7]. She also plans to build a dict keyed by bin location. Explain the choice, and say what would happen if the bins were lists.
2. Write a dict comprehension that maps each order id to its customer name. Show the resulting dict.
3. Using set comprehensions, build the set of customers who ordered on Monday and the set who ordered on Tuesday. Then use set operations to find the customers who ordered on both days and the customers who ordered only on Monday. Show each result, and say why a set suits this job better than a list.
4. Build a dict of lists that groups order ids by customer, for example 'Rosa' mapped to her list of order ids. Use a default pattern so that a customer's first order does not crash the code. Show the result, name the common mistake this avoids, and show how to read Rosa's first order id using indexing.
subParts: Tuple vs list for bin locations
Dict comprehension: id to customer
Set comprehensions and set operations
Grouping into a dict of lists with a default
modelAnswer: A tuple suits bin locations for two reasons. First, (aisle, shelf) is a fixed record whose two positions each have a set meaning, and a location should never be edited in place by accident. Because a tuple is immutable, Python refuses any attempt to change it. Second, immutability makes the tuple hashable, so (3, 7) can be used as a dict key, as in {(3, 7): 'cold storage'}. If the bins were lists, using [3, 7] as a dict key would raise TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'. That error would crash the script that builds the bin lookup. A list can change after it is stored, so Python cannot rely on a fixed fingerprint for it.

id_to_customer = {o['id']: o['customer'] for o in orders}. Tracing it: the loop visits each dict o in turn. For each one it uses o['id'] as the key and o['customer'] as the value. The result is {'A1': 'Rosa', 'A2': 'Theo', 'A3': 'Rosa', 'A4': 'Kemi'}. A lookup such as id_to_customer['A3'] now returns 'Rosa' directly, without searching the list.

mon = {o['customer'] for o in orders if o['day'] == 'Mon'} gives {'Rosa', 'Theo'}. tue = {o['customer'] for o in orders if o['day'] == 'Tue'} gives {'Rosa', 'Kemi'}. Customers on both days come from the intersection, mon & tue (or mon.intersection(tue)), which gives {'Rosa'}. Customers only on Monday come from the difference, mon - tue (or mon.difference(tue)), which gives {'Theo'}. For reference, the union mon | tue gives all three names. A set fits this job for three reasons. It drops duplicates automatically, so a customer appears once however many orders they place. It supports these operations directly. Membership checks such as 'Rosa' in mon are fast. A list would keep repeats and would need manual loops to compare the two days.

Start with an empty dict and loop: by_customer = {} then for o in orders: by_customer.setdefault(o['customer'], []).append(o['id']). setdefault returns the existing list for that customer. If the customer is new, it first stores an empty list and returns that. Tracing it: A1 creates Rosa's list ['A1']. A2 creates ['A2'] for Theo. A3 appends to Rosa's list, giving ['A1', 'A3']. A4 creates ['A4'] for Kemi. The result is {'Rosa': ['A1', 'A3'], 'Theo': ['A2'], 'Kemi': ['A4']}. The common mistake is writing by_customer[o['customer']].append(o['id']) with no default. That raises KeyError the first time a customer is seen, so the script crashes on the very first order. An accepted alternative is a check such as if key not in by_customer: by_customer[key] = [] before appending. Rosa's first order id is by_customer['Rosa'][0], which returns 'A1'. The dict lookup returns her list, and index 0 picks its first item.

scenarios.title: Brightmoor Logistics: the depot report that never complains
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightmoor Logistics, a fictional parcel company, as a junior engineer. Every night a small Python script builds a stock report for each depot (a warehouse). It reads two files. The first is depot.json, a JSON file. JSON is a plain-text format that stores data as name-and-value pairs, much like a Python dictionary. This file should contain a key called depot_code, such as "BRM-07". The second is shipments.csv, a CSV file. CSV means comma-separated values: each line is one record, and commas separate the fields. Each line holds an item name and a quantity, for example:  bolts , 12 

Last week the report showed the depot as UNKNOWN for three nights in a row, and nobody noticed why. Here is the function that reads the JSON file:

import json

def load_depot_code(path):
    try:
        f = open(path)
        data = json.load(f)
        return data["depot_code"]
    except:
        return "UNKNOWN"

Some terms you will need. An exception is an object Python creates, or raises, when something goes wrong while the program runs. If no code handles it, the program stops. A try/except block runs the code under try, and if a matching exception is raised there, it runs the code under except. A bare except is an except line that names no exception type, so it catches every exception. A with statement opens a resource and guarantees it is cleaned up afterwards, for example that a file is closed, even if an error happens. The object that does that cleanup is called a context manager.

Your team lead asks you to do the following.

1. Explain what is wrong with the bare except in this function. Name the specific exception types that the open, json.load and data["depot_code"] steps can raise.

2. Rewrite load_depot_code so it closes the file safely with a with statement and catches only specific exceptions. When a problem happens, it should raise a custom exception called DepotConfigError with a clear message instead of quietly returning UNKNOWN. Show how DepotConfigError is defined.

3. Write a loop that reads shipments.csv and adds up the quantities. It should clean extra spaces from each field, and it should skip any line whose quantity is not a whole number, while recording which line was skipped. Say which exception you catch and why. Use try/except/else so that only successful lines are added to the total.

4. The script finishes by writing summary.txt. Explain what finally would add if the script also had to print "report run finished" every time, whether it succeeded or failed. Explain why the with statement already protects the file without needing a finally.
subParts: Problems with the bare except and the exception types involved
Safe rewrite with with and a custom DepotConfigError
Parsing CSV quantities with a specific except and else
Role of finally versus the with statement
modelAnswer: A bare except catches every exception, so it hides the real cause. A missing file, a corrupted file and a missing key all turn into the same silent UNKNOWN. That is why three bad nights went unnoticed: the program failed, but it never told anyone. A bare except can also swallow problems you never meant to handle, such as a typo in a variable name (NameError) or someone pressing Ctrl+C (KeyboardInterrupt), which makes bugs very hard to find. The function also never closes the file, and if json.load fails, the open file is left behind. The specific types are these. open(path) can raise FileNotFoundError if the file does not exist, or PermissionError if the script may not read it; both are kinds of OSError. json.load(f) can raise json.JSONDecodeError if the text is not valid JSON; this is a kind of ValueError. data["depot_code"] raises KeyError if that key is absent. A good answer names at least FileNotFoundError (or OSError), json.JSONDecodeError and KeyError, and explains that silent failure hides the cause.

Example:

import csv
total = 0
skipped = []
with open("shipments.csv", newline="") as f:
    for line_no, row in enumerate(csv.reader(f), start=1):
        item = row[0].strip()
        qty_text = row[1].strip()
        try:
            qty = int(qty_text)
        except ValueError:
            skipped.append(line_no)
        else:
            total += qty

The csv.reader splits each line on its commas, and strip() removes the extra spaces, so " 12 " becomes "12". You catch ValueError because that is what int() raises when the text is not a whole number, such as "twelve" or "". Only that one bad input is caught, so other bugs are not hidden. The else block runs only when the try succeeded, so the total includes only valid quantities. Recording skipped line numbers means a bad line is visible later instead of disappearing. Tracing " bolts , 12 ": the fields become "bolts" and "12", int gives 12, and else adds 12 to the total. For "nuts, ten": int("ten") raises ValueError, so the line number is added to skipped and the total is unchanged. Using line.split(",") instead of csv.reader is acceptable for this simple file.

A finally block runs after the try and its except or else parts, whether the code succeeded, failed with an exception that was handled, or failed with one that was not. Putting print("report run finished") in finally guarantees the message appears on every run. The error, if any, still carries on afterwards unless it was handled. The with statement already protects summary.txt because the file object is a context manager. When the with block ends, normally or through an exception, the file is closed and any written data is saved to disk. Using with for the file means you do not need a finally just to call close(). Finally is for other actions that must always happen, such as this log message.

scenarios.title: Brightwell Parcels: fixing the fleet classes
subParts: Fix the missing super() call
Composition instead of inheritance for Depot
Add and explain dunder methods
Protect capacity with a property
modelAnswer:
Truck defines its own __init__, which overrides (replaces) Vehicle.__init__. Python does not call the parent's __init__ automatically, so the lines self.plate = plate and self.capacity_kg = capacity_kg never run for a Truck. When describe() calls super().describe(), the parent method reads self.plate, which does not exist, so AttributeError is raised. Fix: call the parent first, then add the child's extra attribute:

def __init__(self, plate, capacity_kg, has_lift):
    super().__init__(plate, capacity_kg)
    self.has_lift = has_lift

Trace: Truck("BW-12", 3000, True) runs Truck.__init__, super().__init__ sets plate to "BW-12" and capacity_kg to 3000, then has_lift is set to True. describe() now returns "Truck BW-12 carries 3000 kg". The class attribute wheels = 6 on Truck correctly overrides the shared value 4 from Vehicle for trucks only.

scenarios.title: Untangling the Shipping Report Project at Larkfield Logistics
scenarios.scenario: You have just joined Larkfield Logistics, a fictional parcel company, as a junior engineer. A teammate, Priya, hands you a small Python project that produces a daily shipping report. Its folder layout is: a top-level folder called shipping_tool containing run.py, plus a subfolder called shiprep. The shiprep folder contains __init__.py (an empty file whose presence marks the folder as importable), parsing.py and summary.py. A module is a single .py file whose code you can load into another file with the import statement. A package is a folder of modules that Python treats as one importable unit. The function load_rows lives in parsing.py, and summary.py needs to call it. The project also uses requests, a third-party library for making web calls. Priya installed requests with pip, Python's tool for downloading and installing outside code, straight into the computer's main Python installation. Now another team project on her laptop, which needs a different version of requests, has stopped working. Your lead asks you to sort things out. A virtual environment (made with Python's built-in venv tool) is a private folder holding its own copy of installed libraries for one project. A requirements.txt file is a plain text list of the libraries, and their exact versions, that a project depends on. A dependency is any outside code a project needs in order to run. Your tasks: 1. Using this project's own files as examples, explain the difference between a module, a package, and a distributed library such as requests. 2. Write the line summary.py should use to import load_rows, once as an absolute import and once as a relative import. Then explain why running python shiprep/summary.py directly makes the relative version fail, and how to run the code so it works. 3. Give the commands to create and activate a virtual environment for this project, install requests at one fixed version, and record that version in requirements.txt. Then say how Priya would recreate the same setup, and why this stops the clash between her two projects. 4. The report must count shipments per destination from a list such as ["Leeds", "York", "Leeds", "Hull", "Leeds", "York"], show the two busiest destinations, and save the result in a reports folder under a filename containing today's date. Name the standard library tools you would use, and trace what the counting step returns for this list.
subParts: Module vs package vs distributed library
Absolute and relative imports
Virtual environment and pinned dependencies
Standard library tools for the report
modelAnswer: A module is one Python file you can import. parsing.py and summary.py are modules, and other code can load load_rows by importing parsing. A package is a folder of modules that Python treats as one unit. shiprep is a package because it contains __init__.py, a file that runs the first time the package is imported and may be empty. A distributed library is code published for other people to download and install, usually from the Python Package Index (PyPI, a public online catalogue), using pip. requests is one. Inside, it is also built from packages and modules, but it is not part of this project's folder. It has to be installed before it can be imported. Standard library modules such as os and datetime are different again: they come with Python itself and need no installing. A good answer contrasts all three and ties each one to a file or folder in this scenario.

Absolute import: from shiprep.parsing import load_rows. This names the full path, starting from the top-level package. Relative import: from .parsing import load_rows. The single dot means 'the package this file is in'. If you run python shiprep/summary.py directly, Python treats summary.py as a standalone script and not as part of the shiprep package. The dot then has no parent package to refer to, and you get an ImportError saying the relative import has no known parent package. To fix it, run the code from the shipping_tool folder: either run python run.py, which imports from the package, or run python -m shiprep.summary, which runs summary as a module inside its package. Running from the project root also puts that folder on sys.path, the list of places Python searches for imports, so the absolute import resolves too.

From inside the shipping_tool folder, create the environment with python -m venv .venv. Activate it with source .venv/bin/activate on macOS or Linux, or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows. Install one exact version, for example pip install requests==2.31.0, then record it with pip freeze > requirements.txt. That writes a line such as requests==2.31.0, along with any libraries requests itself needs. Pinning means fixing an exact version so everyone gets the same code. Priya would create and activate her own .venv in her copy of the project, then run pip install -r requirements.txt. The .venv folder itself should not be shared or committed to version control, because only requirements.txt is needed to rebuild it. This fixes the clash because each project now keeps its libraries in its own environment. Installing or upgrading requests for one project no longer changes the version the other project sees. A common mistake is forgetting to activate the environment, which installs into the main Python installation again and brings the clash back. You can check which environment is active by printing sys.prefix.

Use collections.Counter to tally the destinations, datetime to get today's date, and os to build the file path and create the folder. Code: from collections import Counter; counts = Counter(destinations). Counter goes through the list one item at a time, adding 1 to each name's tally: Leeds 1, York 1, Leeds 2, Hull 1, Leeds 3, York 2. The result is Counter({'Leeds': 3, 'York': 2, 'Hull': 1}). counts.most_common(2) returns [('Leeds', 3), ('York', 2)], the two busiest destinations. For the filename, use datetime.date.today().isoformat() to get text like 2024-05-14. Build the path with os.path.join('reports', 'report_' + date_text + '.txt'), which inserts the correct folder separator for the operating system. Call os.makedirs('reports', exist_ok=True) first so writing the file does not fail when the folder is missing. Full credit needs Counter with the correct traced result and most_common output, plus a reasonable use of datetime and os.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcel Co.: the delivery log that will not fit in memory
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined the data team at Brightwater Parcel Co., a fictional regional delivery company. Every night a file called events.log is written.
